    \[\begin{aligned} &\sum_{\mathrm{e}} \int_0^{h_{\mathrm{e}}} \big(N\,\delta\bar u' + M\,\delta\bar v''\big)\,\mathrm{d}\bar x \\ &\quad = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \int_0^{h_{\mathrm{e}}} \big(\bar q_{\mathrm{x}}\,\delta\bar u + \bar q\,\delta\bar v\big)\,\mathrm{d}\bar x \\ &\quad + \sum_{\mathrm{J}} \big(\vek F_{\mathrm{J}}\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{J}} + M_{\mathrm{J}}\,\delta\varphi_{\mathrm{J}}\big) , \end{aligned} \tag{12.15}\]
    where \(\vek F_{\mathrm{J}}\) is the given load of the node \(J\) (without reactions), \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{J}}\) is the virtual displacement and \(\delta\varphi_{\mathrm{J}}\) the virtual rotation of the node \(J\).
  2. If the only small rigid motion of the whole frame in which the components forbidden at the supports are zero is the zero one, the frame has at most one solution.
Proof

We must show that the boundary terms of the elements add up in the nodes to the work of the node loads (point 1) and that the difference of two solutions is a rigid motion (point 2).

  1. On an element the assumptions of theorem 5.62 hold (continuous functions, \(N' + \bar q_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), \(V' + \bar q = 0\), \(M' + V = 0\)), so by steps 1 to 4 of its proof (the conditions at the ends are needed only for step 5) \(\int_0^{h}(N\,\delta\bar u' + M\,\delta\bar v'')\,\mathrm{d}\bar x = \int_0^{h}(\bar q_{\mathrm{x}}\,\delta\bar u + \bar q\,\delta\bar v)\,\mathrm{d}\bar x + \big[N\,\delta\bar u + V\,\delta\bar v + M\,\delta\bar v'\big]_0^{h}\).
  2. The boundary term of the element is the work of the forces of the surroundings on the nodes on the virtual displacements. By theorem 5.62 the force of the surroundings on node 2 is \((N, V, M)\) at \(\bar x = h\) and on node 1 it is \((-N, -V, -M)\) at \(\bar x = 0\) (definition of the internal force, section 5.2). The boundary term is therefore \(\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{e}}\cdot\delta\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\), the scalar product of the column of forces and the column of virtual displacements of the element, both local.
  3. The scalar product has the same value in every orthogonal Cartesian system (proof of lemma 2.38, point 2), and the moment and the rotation do not change under a rotation of the axes (steps 4 and 5 of the proof of lemma 12.18). Therefore \(\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{e}}\cdot\delta\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\cdot\delta\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) in global components.
  4. Let us add over the elements and collect the terms by nodes. By step 2 of the proof of lemma 5.91 an element with the node \(J\) at its start acts on the piece of the frame around \(J\) with the force \(\bar{\vek F}(0)\), which is the opposite of the force of the surroundings on node 1 of the element. An element with the node \(J\) at its end acts on the piece with the force \(-\bar{\vek F}(h)\), the opposite of the force of the surroundings on node 2. In both cases the force of the element on the piece is the opposite of the force \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\) of the surroundings on the element at \(J\). The equilibrium of the piece (lemma 5.91) is therefore \(\sum_{\mathrm{e} \ni \mathrm{J}}\vek F_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{J}}\), and the same for moments. The sum of boundary terms at \(J\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{e} \ni \mathrm{J}}\big(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{J}} + M_{\mathrm{e}}\,\delta\varphi_{\mathrm{J}}\big) = \vek F_{\mathrm{J}}\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{J}} + M_{\mathrm{J}}\,\delta\varphi_{\mathrm{J}}\), because all elements at \(J\) have the same \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{J}}\) and \(\delta\varphi_{\mathrm{J}}\) (\(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{e}}\) are here the force and moment of the element at \(J\)).
  5. In a node with a support \(\vek F_{\mathrm{J}}\) is the sum of the given force and the reaction. The reaction acts only in the forbidden direction, in which the virtual displacement is zero, so it does no work and the term \(\vek F_{\mathrm{J}}\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{J}}\) contains only the given load. This proves equation (12.15).
  6. Let there be two solutions with the same load and let \(w\) be their difference: fields \(\bar u_{\mathrm{w}}\) and \(\bar v_{\mathrm{w}}\) on the elements. The difference has no load and is an admissible virtual displacement (continuity, supports). Equation (12.15) with \(\delta = w\) and a zero right side gives \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\int_0^{h_{\mathrm{e}}}\big(EA\,\bar u_{\mathrm{w}}'^2 + EI\,\bar v_{\mathrm{w}}''^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}\bar x = 0\). The integrand is nonnegative and continuous, so \(\bar u_{\mathrm{w}}' = 0\) and \(\bar v_{\mathrm{w}}'' = 0\) on each element (as in step 2 of lemma 6.7), hence \(\bar u_{\mathrm{w}}\) is a constant and \(\bar v_{\mathrm{w}}\) a linear function (corollary 1.85).
  7. An element with a constant \(\bar u_{\mathrm{w}}\) and a linear \(\bar v_{\mathrm{w}}\) moves as a rigid body (definition 1.11): the point of its axis at \(\bar x\) is displaced by \((\bar u_{\mathrm{w}},\ \bar v_{\mathrm{w}}(0) + \varphi\,\bar x)\) with \(\varphi = \bar v_{\mathrm{w}}'\), which is the displacement of the point at \(\bar x = 0\) plus the rotation \(\varphi\) about it, that is a field of the form \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) from theorem 1.134, in the plane \(\vek u = (a_1 - \varphi\,y,\ a_2 + \varphi\,x)\). Such a field is determined by the displacement of one point and the rotation \(\varphi\). Two elements in a common node have the same displacement and rotation of the node, so their rigid motion is the same. A connected frame therefore moves as one whole, that is as a small rigid motion of the frame, which by assumption is zero because of the supports. The difference \(w\) is zero, so the solution is unique.

Source: The proof is not from a source. The principle of virtual displacements of the frame is in chapter 5 (corollary 5.92, steps 1 to 4), and uniqueness from energy has the form of the proof of theorem 5.49.

Equation (12.15) is the frame form of the principle of virtual displacements of a beam (theorem 5.62): we collected the boundary terms of the elements by nodes, as for the unit load (corollary 5.92), only here it holds for every admissible virtual displacement. Now we show that the assembled system is really the frame.

Theorem 12.20 Finite element method for a plane frame (metoda končnih elementov za ravninski okvir)

Let a plane frame (definition 5.90) be divided into frame elements (definition 12.17) with constant \(EA\) and \(EI\) on each element, let it be connected, and let it have supports and loads as in lemma 12.19. Let the only small rigid motion of the frame in which the forbidden components are zero be the zero one. Let \(\mat K\) and \(\vek f\) be the matrix and the right side of the frame from theorem 7.13 with the matrices \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) from lemma 12.18 and the consistent forces \(\vek f_{\mathrm{e}}\) (point 3 of the lemma), and let \(\vek P\) be the column of external forces and moments of the nodes in the directions of the unknowns. For each element let \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} - \vek f_{\mathrm{e}}\). Then:

  1. The row of a free displacement or rotation of the node \(J\) of the system \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f\) is the equilibrium of the joint from lemma 5.91, \(\sum_{\mathrm{e} \ni \mathrm{J}}\vek F_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{J}}\) (component by component).
  2. The reduced system (theorem 7.18) has exactly one solution \(\vek d\).
  3. The displacements and rotations of the nodes of this solution are exactly the displacements and rotations of the solution of the frame, and \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the column of forces and moments that the surroundings exert on the nodes of the element in the solution of the frame, so \(\mat R\,\vek F_{\mathrm{e}} = (-N, -V, -M, N, V, M)^\T\) in local components, with the values at \(\bar x = 0\) for the first three and at \(\bar x = h\) for the last three. If there is no load on the elements, the field of the element \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}\), \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}\) is a solution of the frame, so the displacement is exact along the whole length.
Proof

We must show that the rows of the system give the equilibrium of the nodes (point 1), that the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is positive definite (point 2), and that by recomputing the end forces and correcting the field we obtain a solution of the frame, which is unique by lemma 12.19 (point 3).

  1. By point 1 of theorem 7.13 row \(I\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}}(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{i}} = f_{\mathrm{I}} = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} (\vek f_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{i}} + P_{\mathrm{I}}\), where \(P_{\mathrm{I}}\) is the component of the external force or moment of the node in the direction of the unknown \(I\). So \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}}(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} - \vek f_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{i}} = P_{\mathrm{I}}\), which is \(\sum_{\mathrm{e} \ni \mathrm{J}}\vek F_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{J}}\) by components. By step 4 of the proof of lemma 12.19 this is the equilibrium of the joint.
  2. Let \(\vek d\) be a column with zero prescribed unknowns and \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = 0\). By point 2 of theorem 7.13 \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\), each term is \(2U_{\mathrm{e}} \ge 0\) (lemma 12.18, point 2, with \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) symmetric, so the hypothesis of corollary 7.14 holds for \(\mat K\)), so \(U_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\) for every element. The energy is the sum \(\tfrac12\int(EA\,\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}'^2 + EI\,\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}''^2)\), so \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}\) is constant and \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}\) linear, as in steps 6 and 7 of lemma 12.19, the elements move rigidly, the frame as a whole rigidly, and by assumption \(\vek d = \vek 0\). By theorem 7.18 the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is positive definite and the system has exactly one solution.
  3. Let \(\vek d\) be this solution and \(\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) the local displacements of each element. For each element let us define the fields \(\bar u = \bar u_{\mathrm{h}} + \bar u_0\) and \(\bar v = \bar v_{\mathrm{h}} + \bar v_0\), where \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}\), \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}\) are the finite element fields from \(\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\), \(\bar u_0\) is the solution of the equation \(EA\,\bar u_0'' = -\bar q_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\bar v_0\) the solution of the equation \(EI\,\bar v_0'''' = \bar q\), both with the value zero at both ends of the element, \(\bar v_0\) also with zero slope at both ends. Such functions exist and are unique: the second or fourth derivative is known, by theorem 5.45 the solution is determined up to a polynomial of degree at most 1 or 3, and the conditions determine the polynomial exactly (a line through two points, a cubic polynomial by lemma 12.2). Without a load \(\bar u_0 = 0\), \(\bar v_0 = 0\).
  4. The fields \(\bar u\), \(\bar v\) satisfy condition 1 of the solution of the frame: \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}'' = 0\) and \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}'''' = 0\) (a linear and a cubic function), so \(N' = EA\,\bar u'' = EA\,\bar u_0'' = -\bar q_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(V' = -M'' = -EI\,\bar v'''' = -EI\,\bar v_0'''' = -\bar q\).
  5. Condition 2: \(\bar u_0\) and \(\bar v_0\) are zero at both ends of the element with zero slope, so \(\bar u\) and \(\bar v\) have at the ends the same values and slope as \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}\) and \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}\), that is the displacements and rotations of the nodes of the solution \(\vek d\). These are equal for elements in the same node. Supports: the forbidden components are zero in \(\vek d\).
  6. The forces of the surroundings on the nodes of the element for the fields \(\bar u\), \(\bar v\) are the sum of the forces of the fields \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}\), \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}\) and the forces of the fields \(\bar u_0\), \(\bar v_0\). The first are by lemma 12.18 (point 1) equal to \(\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\), because \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}\) and \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}\) are fields of an element without a load. The second are \(-\bar{\vek f}_{\mathrm{e}}\). For the axial part this follows from lemma 7.9 applied to \(\bar u_0\) with zero node displacements (\(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\cdot\vek 0 = \vek f_{\mathrm{e}} + \vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\)). For the bending part \(\int_0^h EI\,\bar v_0''\,H_{\mathrm{i}}''\,\mathrm{d}\bar x = 0\) holds for each Hermite function \(H_{\mathrm{i}}\): after integration by parts a boundary term with \(\bar v_0'\) remains, which is zero at the ends, and the integral \(-EI\,H_{\mathrm{i}}'''\int_0^h \bar v_0'\,\mathrm{d}\bar x = -EI\,H_{\mathrm{i}}'''\,\big(\bar v_0(h) - \bar v_0(0)\big) = 0\), since \(H_{\mathrm{i}}'''\) is constant. Therefore by theorem 5.62 with the virtual displacement \(H_{\mathrm{i}}\) the work of the forces of the surroundings at the ends is \(-\int_0^h \bar q\,H_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}\bar x = -(\bar f_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{i}}\) (corollary 12.15, point 3). The sum is \(\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} - \bar{\vek f}_{\mathrm{e}}\), and by lemma 12.18 (points 2 and 3) this is in global components \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} - \vek f_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  7. By point 1 and step 6 \(\sum_{\mathrm{e} \ni \mathrm{J}}\vek F_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{J}}\) holds in the nodes, so condition 3 of the solution of the frame. By steps 4 to 6 \((\bar u, \bar v)\) is therefore a solution of the frame. By lemma 12.19 it is unique, so this is the solution of the frame, its node displacements and rotations are \(\vek d\) and the forces at the ends of the elements are \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\). Without a load \(\bar u_0 = 0\) and \(\bar v_0 = 0\), so the solution is the finite element field.

Source: COOK §2.5 (PDF pp. 46-47), where each node is a small joint in equilibrium under the forces of the elements and the external load, ONATE2 (PDF pp. 49-50), where for a beam with forces only in the nodes the finite element field is exact. The proof is not from a source.

The theorem has two conditions that we must not forget. The first is a constant \(EI\) (and \(EA\)) on each element, the second consistent forces for a load on an element (section 12.2). If \(EI\) varied inside an element or if we replaced the load by crude forces in the nodes, for example by half of the weight on each node without moments, the nodal values would no longer be exact, as section 12.3 shows. The proof also showed what remains inside the element: the true displacement is the finite element field plus the displacement \(\bar v_0\) of an element clamped at both ends, so the field itself is exact only without a load on the element.

We treat supports as for the bar, with the division of the unknowns into free and prescribed (theorem 7.18). The reaction in a prescribed unknown is the value \((\mat K\,\vek d - \vek f)_{\mathrm{I}}\) in the row of this unknown (section 7.3.4), that is the sum of the forces of the surroundings \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\) on the elements in the node in this direction, which the support must provide. A hinge (členek) between two elements is modelled so that each element has its own rotation unknown in the node, and the displacements are common: the connectivity table (definition 7.10) has two numbers for the rotation in the node. The row of each of these two unknowns is by point 1 of theorem 7.13 the moment of one element and demands that the moment of this element in the hinge is zero, as figure 5.78 shows. Theorem 12.20 is proved for rigid joints, so we do not prove uniqueness of the solution with a hinge, but we check it with statics in the example at the end of the section.

The rotations of the nodes as unknowns have their history, which Timoshenko tells and which begins with reinforced concrete.

From history

The theory of structures was developed in the nineteenth century principally for trusses, since for trusses satisfactory solutions were obtained by assuming that the joints are hinged and that all bars are loaded only axially (TIMO, PDF p. 361). With the introduction of reinforced concrete into structural engineering, various frame structures spread. These are usually highly statically indeterminate and their elements work mostly in bending, so the previously developed methods soon proved unsuitable and new ones were introduced, based on deformations (TIMO, PDF p. 361). Timoshenko points out that already in the computation of secondary stresses it is useful to take the rotations of rigid joints as unknowns (TIMO, PDF p. 361). The systematic use of rotations in the analysis of frames, however, was introduced by Axel Bendixen, who developed the slope-deflection method (metoda zasukov), and his book was published in Berlin in 1914 (TIMO, PDF p. 361, note 1). His equation writes the moment at the end \(m\) of the element \(mn\) as twice the stiffness factor \(k = EI/l\) multiplied by the sum of twice the rotation of the end \(m\) and the rotation of the end \(n\), plus the fixed-end moment. This is the moment that would act on the end \(m\) if both ends were fixed and only transverse forces acted on the element. Rotations and moments are positive clockwise in this equation (TIMO, PDF p. 361). He uses the equation for frames in which the displacements of the joints can be neglected, and treats more general cases in his paper (TIMO, PDF p. 361, note 2). If at the joint \(a\), where four elements meet, we took the moments at the ends of the elements as unknowns, we would have to derive and solve seven equations, and with the rotation \(\theta_{\mathrm{a}}\) of the joint as the unknown the computation reduces to one equation, which we obtain by setting the sum of the four moments at the ends of the elements in the joint equal to zero (TIMO, PDF p. 362). With several joints one such equation is written for each, the number of equations equals the number of unknown rotations, and when the rotations are computed, all the moments at the ends are known from the equation for the moment (TIMO, PDF p. 362). The next step of simplification was made by K. A. Čališev, who used successive approximations and so solved in each step one equation with one unknown (TIMO, PDF p. 362). He first assumed that all joints are fixed and do not rotate under load, calculated the fixed-end moments for all loaded elements and summed them by joints. This sum with a negative sign is the unbalanced moment of the joint (TIMO, PDF p. 362). Then he unlocked one joint at a time, leaving the others fixed, and for the unlocked joint computed the first approximation of the rotation with an equation similar to Bendixen's (TIMO, PDF pp. 362-363). He recommended beginning at the joint with the largest unbalanced moment (TIMO, PDF p. 362, note 2). The same aim can also be reached by distributing the unbalanced moments directly while unlocking one joint at a time and holding the others fixed. This procedure of successive approximations was proposed by Hardy Cross and found wide use in America (TIMO, PDF p. 363, note).

We were looking at how frames with several rigid joints were computed with the rotations of the joints as unknowns. Our row of the system for the rotation of a joint is exactly Bendixen's joint equation: the sum of the moments at the ends of the elements in the joint equals the external moment (point 1 of theorem 12.20). The moment that the surroundings exert on end 1 of the element when \(\bar v_1 = \bar v_2\) is the third row of the matrix (12.12), \(\tfrac{4EI}{h}\,\varphi_1 + \tfrac{2EI}{h}\,\varphi_2 = 2k\,(2\varphi_1 + \varphi_2)\) with \(k = EI/h\). We wrote the equation with rotations counterclockwise, and when the direction is reversed the signs of rotations and moments are reversed and the form of the equation does not change. The stiffness factors of the classical method are therefore the entries \(4EI/h\) and \(2EI/h\) of the element matrix. The fixed-end moment is for us the moment that the surroundings exert on an element fixed at both ends, that is \(-\bar f_3\) at \(\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\) (corollary 12.15, point 3).

12.4.3 L-frame (okvir L)

We divide the L-frame of section 5.14.2 (figure 5.79) into two elements, the column \(AB\) and the crossbeam \(BC\), each with \(h = 1\) m. We number the nodes \(A = 1\), \(B = 2\), \(C = 3\) and each has three unknowns, nine in all: \(\vek d = (u_{\mathrm{A}}, v_{\mathrm{A}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{A}}, u_{\mathrm{B}}, v_{\mathrm{B}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{B}}, u_{\mathrm{C}}, v_{\mathrm{C}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{C}})\). The column has the nodes \((A, B)\) and the angle \(\alpha = \pi/2\) (a right angle), so \(c = 0\), \(s = 1\), \(\mat Q = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\): the local axial displacement \(\bar u\) is the global \(v\), the local transverse \(\bar v\) is \(-u\) (the local axis \(\bar y\) points to the left, as in chapter 5). The crossbeam has the nodes \((B, C)\), the angle \(\alpha = 0\) and \(\mat Q = \mat I\). The connectivity table (definition 7.10) has the rows \((1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)\) and \((4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9)\). At \(A\) there is a clamp (definition 5.5), so the unknowns 1 to 3 are prescribed and equal to zero, at \(C\) acts the force \(F = 500\) N downward, \(f_8 = -500\) N, and there are no other loads. There are six free unknowns. We assemble the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) by theorem 7.13 from the matrices \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R^\T\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\mat R\) from lemma 12.18 with the values that we computed above. For the unknowns \((u_{\mathrm{B}}, v_{\mathrm{B}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{B}}, u_{\mathrm{C}}, v_{\mathrm{C}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{C}})\) we get (units \(10^5\) for N/m, N and N m)

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}} = 10^5 \begin{bmatrix} 1570{,}51 & 0 & 1{,}2544 & -1568 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1570{,}51 & 1{,}2544 & 0 & -2{,}5088 & 1{,}2544 \\ 1{,}2544 & 1{,}2544 & 1{,}67253 & 0 & -1{,}2544 & 0{,}418133 \\ -1568 & 0 & 0 & 1568 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2{,}5088 & -1{,}2544 & 0 & 2{,}5088 & -1{,}2544 \\ 0 & 1{,}2544 & 0{,}418133 & 0 & -1{,}2544 & 0{,}836267 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The entry \((1, 1)\) is the sum of the axial stiffness of the crossbeam, \(1568\cdot 10^5\) N/m, and the transverse stiffness of the column, \(2{,}5088\cdot 10^5\) N/m, because the horizontal displacement of the node \(B\) appears as transverse for the column and as axial for the crossbeam. The entry \((2, 2)\) is the same sum with the roles exchanged. The entry \((3, 3)\) is the sum of the stiffnesses \(4EI/h = 0{,}836267\cdot 10^5\) N m of both elements, because the rotation of the node \(B\) bends both. The solution of the system \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} = (0, 0, 0, 0, -500, 0)^\T\) N is (NumPy)

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{B}} = u_{\mathrm{C}} &= 11{,}9579\ \text{mm} , & v_{\mathrm{B}} &= -0{,}00319\ \text{mm} , & v_{\mathrm{C}} &= -31{,}8909\ \text{mm} , \\ \varphi_{\mathrm{B}} &= -0{,}023916 , & \varphi_{\mathrm{C}} &= -0{,}035874 . \end{aligned}\]

From chapter 5 we know \(u_{\mathrm{C}} = 11{,}96\) mm, \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = -31{,}89\) mm and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}} = -0{,}02392\). The displacement \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\) with the axial term by equation (5.83) is \(-(7{,}9719 + 23{,}9158 + 0{,}0032)\ \text{mm} = -31{,}8909\) mm and the system gives exactly this. The displacement \(v_{\mathrm{B}} = -0{,}00319\) mm is the axial shortening of the column, \(F a/EA = 0{,}0032\) mm. The deformed shape, assembled from the fields of both elements, is shown in figure 12.12. The solution is the same up to rounding, because the load is only in a node and so by theorem 12.20 the finite element field is exactly the solution of the frame.

The forces at the ends of the elements we obtain from \(\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{e}} = \bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\), where \(\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\). For the column \(\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} = (0,\ 0,\ 0,\ -0{,}00319\ \text{mm},\ -11{,}9579\ \text{mm},\ -0{,}023916)\) (the local transverse displacement is \(\bar v_2 = -u_{\mathrm{B}}\)), for the crossbeam \((11{,}9579\ \text{mm},\ -0{,}00319\ \text{mm},\ -0{,}023916,\ 11{,}9579\ \text{mm},\ -31{,}8909\ \text{mm},\ -0{,}035874)\). With the element matrix we get

\[\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{AB}} = (500,\ 0,\ 500,\ -500,\ 0,\ -500)^\T , \qquad \bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{BC}} = (0,\ 500,\ 500,\ 0,\ -500,\ 0)^\T\]

in N and N m. By lemma 12.18 this is \((-N, -V, -M)\) at \(\bar x = 0\) and \((N, V, M)\) at \(\bar x = h\). For the column we therefore have \(N = -500\) N, \(V = 0\) and \(M = -500\) N m at both ends, for the crossbeam \(V = -500\) N and \(M = -500\) N m at \(B\) and \(0\) at \(C\). These are the values from section 5.14.2: the axial force of the column is \(-F\), the moment of the column is \(-F b\) and the moment of the crossbeam is \(-F\,(b - s)\). Let us also check the equilibrium of the node \(B\) by lemma 5.91 and point 1 of theorem 12.20. The force of the surroundings on the column at \(B\) is in local components \((-500, 0)\), in global components \(\mat Q^\T(-500, 0)^\T = (0, -500)\) N, the force of the surroundings on the crossbeam at \(B\) is \((0, 500)\) N, the sum is zero, and the moments \(-500\) and \(+500\) N m give zero. The reaction at \(A\) is the force of the surroundings on the column at node 1, globally \(\mat Q^\T(500, 0)^\T = (0, 500)\) N and the moment \(+500\) N m, which is the equilibrium of the whole frame (\(F\,b = 500\) N m about \(A\) counterclockwise).

12.4.4 Truss with welded joints (paličje z zvarjenimi vozlišči)

The truss of section 5.14.3 has the bars \(AC\) (\(4\) m) and \(BC\) (\(5\) m), \(A = (-4, 0)\), \(B = (-4, 3)\), \(C = (0, 0)\), clamped at \(A\) and \(B\) and rigidly welded at \(C\), with a load of \(10\) kN downward at \(C\). The nodes are \(A = 1\), \(B = 2\), \(C = 3\), there are nine unknowns, only the unknowns of the node \(C\) are free and the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is the \(3 \times 3\) block of the node \(C\). The bar \(AC\) has \(C\) as node 2, angle \(0\), so \(c = 1\), \(s = 0\). The bar \(BC\) has the vector \((4, -3)\) m, so \(h = 5\) m, \(c = 0{,}8\), \(s = -0{,}6\), and also has \(C\) as node 2. Both elements therefore contribute the block \(\mat k_{22}\) from equation (12.14) and the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is their sum (theorem 7.13, point 1, the rows of the node \(C\) have only these two elements). Figure 12.13 shows where the blocks of both elements go.

The bar \(AC\) has \(EA/h = 4{,}9\cdot 10^6\) N/m, \(12EI/h^3 = 30{,}625\) N/m, \(6EI/h^2 = 61{,}25\) N and \(4EI/h = 163{,}33\) N m. With \(c = 1\), \(s = 0\) by equation (12.14)

\[\mat k_{22}^{AC} = \begin{bmatrix} 4{,}9\cdot 10^6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 30{,}625 & -61{,}25 \\ 0 & -61{,}25 & 163{,}33 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The bar \(BC\) has \(EA/h = 3{,}92\cdot 10^6\) N/m, \(12EI/h^3 = 15{,}68\) N/m, \(6EI/h^2 = 39{,}2\) N and \(4EI/h = 130{,}67\) N m. With \(c = 0{,}8\), \(s = -0{,}6\) the first entry is \(c^2\,EA/h + s^2\,12EI/h^3 = 0{,}64\cdot 3{,}92\cdot 10^6 + 0{,}36\cdot 15{,}68 = 2{,}5088\cdot 10^6\) N/m, the second \(c\,s\,(EA/h - 12EI/h^3) = -0{,}48\cdot(3{,}92\cdot 10^6 - 15{,}68) = -1{,}8816\cdot 10^6\) N/m, the third (row \(v\), column \(v\)) \(0{,}36\cdot 3{,}92\cdot 10^6 + 0{,}64\cdot 15{,}68 = 1{,}41121\cdot 10^6\) N/m, and the entries with the rotation \(6EI/h^2\,s = -23{,}52\) N and \(-6EI/h^2\,c = -31{,}36\) N. So

\[\mat k_{22}^{BC} = \begin{bmatrix} 2{,}5088\cdot 10^6 & -1{,}8816\cdot 10^6 & -23{,}52 \\ -1{,}8816\cdot 10^6 & 1{,}41121\cdot 10^6 & -31{,}36 \\ -23{,}52 & -31{,}36 & 130{,}67 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The sum \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}} = \mat k_{22}^{AC} + \mat k_{22}^{BC}\) is

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}} = \begin{bmatrix} 7{,}4088\cdot 10^6 & -1{,}8816\cdot 10^6 & -23{,}52 \\ -1{,}8816\cdot 10^6 & 1{,}41124\cdot 10^6 & -92{,}61 \\ -23{,}52 & -92{,}61 & 294{,}0 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

which is up to rounding the matrix (5.86) of chapter 5 (\(7{,}409\cdot 10^6\), \(-1{,}882\cdot 10^6\), \(1{,}411\cdot 10^6\), \(-23{,}52\), \(-92{,}61\), \(294{,}0\)). The entry \((2, 3)\) is \(-61{,}25 - 31{,}36 = -92{,}61\) and the entry \((3, 3)\) is \(163{,}33 + 130{,}67 = 294{,}0\). Chapter 5 assembled the matrix by hand from lemma 5.93, that is from the inverted flexibility matrix of a cantilever. Now we know why the result is the same: the inverted matrix of the cantilever is the lower right block of the beam element matrix (lemma 12.4, point 3), in the matrix (12.12) the block of node 2, which the rotation with \(\mat R_2\) converts into global axes, and the sum over the elements is the equilibrium of the joint from lemma 5.91.

The solution of the system \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} = (0, -10\,000, 0)^\T\) (NumPy) is \(u_{\mathrm{C}} = -2{,}7211\) mm, \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = -10{,}7142\) mm, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{C}} = -3{,}5926\cdot 10^{-3}\), which agrees with chapter 5 (\(-2{,}721\) mm, \(-10{,}714\) mm, \(-3{,}593\cdot 10^{-3}\)). The forces at the ends of the elements \(\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{e}} = \bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) give the axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -13\,333{,}2\) N and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 16\,666{,}5\) N and the moments \(M = -0{,}3628\) N m at \(A\) and \(0{,}0694\) N m at \(C\) on the bar \(AC\), and \(-0{,}1653\) N m at \(B\) and \(-0{,}0694\) N m at \(C\) on the bar \(BC\). The moments in the node \(C\) have the sum zero, as lemma 5.91 demands, because there is no external moment at \(C\). These are the values of chapter 5 (\(-13{,}333\) and \(16{,}666\) kN, \(-0{,}363\), \(0{,}069\), \(-0{,}165\) and \(-0{,}069\) N m). The promise at the end of the section on the welded truss is fulfilled: the general method that assembles the matrix for any number of elements and nodes as (5.86) is now determined in theorem 12.20.

12.4.5 Statically indeterminate frame (statično nedoločen okvir)

Chapter 5 solved the statically indeterminate frame by choosing the unknown reaction \(R\) at \(C\), writing the complementary energy and demanding \(\partial U^*/\partial R = 0\) (section 5.14.4). In the finite element method we choose nothing: the unknowns are always the displacements and rotations of the nodes, and a support only prescribes one of them. We divide the same frame, with a load \(F = 500\) N in the middle of the crossbeam and a roller support at \(C\) (definition 5.5), into three elements: the column \(AB\) and two halves of the crossbeam, \(BD\) and \(DC\) with \(h = 0{,}5\) m, so that the force acts at the node \(D\) and we do not need consistent forces. The nodes \(A\), \(B\), \(D\), \(C\) have 12 unknowns together. Four are prescribed: the clamp at \(A\) gives \(u_{\mathrm{A}} = v_{\mathrm{A}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{A}} = 0\) and the support at \(C\) gives \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\). The vertical displacement is an unknown of the node \(C\), so the support only prescribes the unknown, without any other consideration. There are eight free ones, the right side has the only nonzero entry \(f_{\mathrm{v}_\mathrm{D}} = -500\) N.

The reaction \(R\) is by section 7.3.4 the value \((\mat K\,\vek d - \vek f)\) in the row of the prescribed unknown \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\). The solution (NumPy) gives \(R = 226{,}590\) N upward. Chapter 5 with the model without axial extension obtained \(R = F\,\dfrac{5b + 24a}{16\,(b + 3a)} = 226{,}5625\) N and with the axial term \(226{,}59\) N. If in the same computation we increase \(EA\) a million times, we get \(226{,}5625\) N, so the model without axial extension exactly, and \(226{,}590\) N with the true \(EA\). The difference is \(0{,}012\) %. The other quantities are \(u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0{,}5599\) mm (chapter 5 \(0{,}561\) mm without the axial term), the vertical force in the clamp \(273{,}41\) N, the reaction moment in the clamp \(23{,}410\) N m counterclockwise, so the internal moment of the column is \(-23{,}410\) N m (chapter 5 \(-23{,}44\) N m), and the moment under the load \(113{,}295\) N m. The nodes \(B\), \(D\) and \(C\) have the same horizontal displacement \(0{,}5599\) mm, because there is no axial force in the crossbeam (there is no horizontal force in the column).

Figure 12.14 shows the mesh and the moment that we get from the forces at the ends of the elements. These are in N and N m \(\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{AB}} = (273{,}41,\ 0,\ 23{,}410,\ -273{,}41,\ 0,\ -23{,}410)\), \(\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{BD}} = (0,\ 273{,}41,\ 23{,}410,\ 0,\ -273{,}41,\ 113{,}295)\) and \(\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{DC}} = (0,\ -226{,}59,\ -113{,}295,\ 0,\ 226{,}59,\ 0)\). By lemma 12.18 we therefore have in the column \(N = -273{,}41\) N (compression, as \(R - F\) in chapter 5), \(V = 0\) and \(M = -23{,}410\) N m. In the left half of the crossbeam \(V = -273{,}41\) N and the moment grows from \(-23{,}410\) N m at \(B\) to \(113{,}295\) N m under the load, because \(M' = -V\). In the right half \(V = +226{,}59\) N and the moment falls to \(0\) at \(C\). The jump of the transverse force under the load is \(226{,}59 - (-273{,}41) = 500\) N, as lemma 5.12 demands for a force \(500\) N downward.

The difference between \(226{,}590\) and \(226{,}5625\) N tells what the model of chapter 5 left out: the axial extension of the column and the crossbeam. The finite element method takes it along without extra work, because the axial stiffness \(EA\) is part of the matrix of each element. The price is eight unknowns instead of one, which is no trouble for a computer.

12.4.6 Load on an element and a hinge (breme na elementu in členek)

Until now the load was always at a node. What if it acts along an element? Let us take the L-frame of section 12.4.3 with a constant horizontal load \(w = 1000\) N/m in the direction \(+x\) (wind) along the whole height \(a = 1\) m of the column \(AB\) and no force at \(C\). The column is one element, the crossbeam another. The local axis \(\bar y\) of the column points in the direction \(-x\), so the local transverse load is \(\bar q = -w\). The consistent forces from section 12.2 are \(\bar{\vek f}_{\mathrm{e}} = -w\,(0,\ h/2,\ h^2/12,\ 0,\ h/2,\ -h^2/12) = (0,\ -500,\ -83{,}33,\ 0,\ -500,\ 83{,}33)\) in N and N m, and by lemma 12.18 (point 3) \(\vek f_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R^\T\bar{\vek f}_{\mathrm{e}} = (500,\ 0,\ -83{,}33,\ 500,\ 0,\ 83{,}33)\). At the nodes \(A\) and \(B\) there are therefore forces of \(500\) N each in the direction \(+x\), half of the load \(w\,a\) on each node, and the moments \(\mp 83{,}33\) N m, which ensure that the forces and couples on every Hermite field of the element do the same work as the load (lemma 12.7).

The solution (NumPy) gives \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = 5{,}9790\) mm, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}} = -7{,}9719\cdot 10^{-3}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = -7{,}9719\) mm. The exact values follow from chapter 5. The moment of the load on the part of the column above the section at \(s\) is \(M(s) = -w\,(a - s)^2/2\). A unit moment at \(B\) (\(m = 1\)) gives \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}} = \int_0^a M/EI\,\mathrm{d}s = -w\,a^3/(6EI) = -7{,}9719\cdot 10^{-3}\), a unit horizontal force at \(B\) (\(m = -(a - s)\)) gives \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = \int_0^a m\,M/EI\,\mathrm{d}s = w\,a^4/(8EI) = 5{,}9790\) mm. The crossbeam without a load rotates as a rigid body, so \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{B}}\,b = -7{,}9719\) mm. The forces on node 1 of the column are \(\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{e}} = \bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} - \bar{\vek f}_{\mathrm{e}}\), locally \(\bar F_2 = 1000\) N and \(\bar F_3 = 500\) N m. Therefore \(V(0) = -\bar F_2 = -w\,a = -1000\) N and \(M(0) = -\bar F_3 = -w\,a^2/2 = -500\) N m, which are the transverse force and the moment of the load above the section at \(s = 0\). Theorem 12.20 (point 3) therefore holds up to rounding: the nodal values and the forces at the ends of the elements are exact.

Inside the element the finite element field is not exact. At the middle of the column the field \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}\) moves in the direction \(+x\) by \(1{,}9930\) mm, and the true displacement is \(w\,s^2(6a^2 - 4a\,s + s^2)/(24EI) = 2{,}1175\) mm at \(s = a/2\). The difference \(0{,}1246\) mm is \(w\,a^4/(384EI)\), which is the correction \(\bar v_0\) from the proof of theorem 12.20 at the middle of the element. If we divide the column into two elements, the error at the middle of each is 16 times smaller, because \(h^4\) decreases by 16 (section 12.3).

What remains is the hinge. Let us take the statically indeterminate frame of the previous section, but with a hinge at \(B\) between the column and the crossbeam. The node \(B\) now has four unknowns: \(u_{\mathrm{B}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{B}}\), the rotation of the column \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}^{(1)}\) and the rotation of the crossbeam \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}^{(2)}\), so there are 13 unknowns in all, the same four are prescribed as before, and nine are free. The connectivity table of the column is \((1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)\), of the first half of the crossbeam \((4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10)\) and of the second \((8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13)\). The solution (NumPy) is \(R = 250{,}000\) N, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}^{(1)} = 0\), \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}^{(2)} = -1{,}4931\cdot 10^{-3}\) and the moment under the load \(125{,}000\) N m. Statics confirms this. At the hinge the moment is zero, so the crossbeam is a simply supported beam of length 1 m with the force \(F\) in the middle, with the reaction \(F/2 = 250\) N at each support and the moment \(F\,L/4 = 125\) N m under the force. The column carries only the axial force \(-250\) N and does not bend, so \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}^{(1)} = 0\). The rotation of the crossbeam at \(B\) for a simply supported beam is \(-F L^2/(16EI) = -1{,}4947\cdot 10^{-3}\). The difference \(1{,}6\cdot 10^{-6}\) is the vertical displacement of the node \(B\), \(v_{\mathrm{B}} = -0{,}00159\) mm (the column shortens by \(250\ \text{N}\cdot 1\ \text{m}/EA\)), divided by the length of the crossbeam, because the chord of the crossbeam therefore rotates.

Let us summarize. The frame element is the sum of the bar element and the beam element, rotated with the matrix \(\mat R\) (lemma 12.18). In each node it has three unknowns, a displacement and a rotation, as the frame demands (definition 5.90). The rows of the assembled system are the equilibrium of the nodes, the solution is unique and is the solution of the frame exactly at the nodes, and for loads only in the nodes along the whole length (theorem 12.20). The same procedure gave all three frames of chapter 5 and did not require us to choose a reaction or to compute a displacement with a unit force. A hinge, a rigid connection and a support differ only in the connectivity table and in the prescribed unknowns, the element matrices are the same everywhere.

12.5 The space frame (prostorski okvir)

In section 5.14.5 of chapter 5 we turned the L-frame out of the plane. The force \(F = 500\) N acts in the direction of the axis \(Y\), perpendicular to the plane of the frame, and we obtained the six internal forces from equilibrium (the table in that section). How far does the point \(C\) move? Equilibrium does not tell, because the displacement is determined by stiffness. By that table the column has the torque \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = F\,b = 500\) N m along its whole length, so it twists, and the displacement of the point \(C\) depends on how the cross section resists twisting. Besides \(EA\), \(EI_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(EI_{\mathrm{z}}\) we need one more stiffness, the torsional one.

The plane frame (section 12.4) gave the procedure: the element in local axes, the turn into global axes, assembly and the reduced system. In space the procedure stays the same, but three things change. The element has six unknowns at each node instead of three. Bending happens in two planes. The rotation of a node is no longer a number but a vector, which has to be mapped when the axes are turned. The section therefore first sets up the model and the unknowns, then builds the element matrix, then shows that the rotation is mapped with the same matrix as the displacement, then says that the solution is again exact at the nodes, and finally computes the L-frame.

12.5.1 Model and unknowns of the element

The element is a straight beam with its axis through the centroids of the sections. The local axis \(\bar x\) runs along the element from node 1 towards node 2, the local axes \(\bar y\) and \(\bar z\) are the principal axes of the section (corollary 5.31) and the triple \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\), \(\bar z\) is right-handed. Bending in the plane \(\bar x\bar y\) is the Euler-Bernoulli bending of chapter 5 with the moment of inertia \(I_{\mathrm{z}} = \int \bar y^2\,\mathrm{d}A\), and bending in the plane \(\bar x\bar z\) is the same theory with \(I_{\mathrm{y}} = \int \bar z^2\,\mathrm{d}A\) (section 5.14.5). The axial displacement \(\bar u\) and the transverse displacements \(\bar v\) (in the direction \(\bar y\)) and \(\bar w\) (in the direction \(\bar z\)) are displacements of the element axis.

Torsion needs a model that chapter 5 did not have. We assume uniform torsion (enakomerna torzija): the sections rotate about the axis of the element by the angle \(\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}(\bar x)\) and in doing so may freely bulge out of their plane (warping of the section, zvitje prereza: sections free to warp). A transverse force that passes through the centroid does not rotate the section. For a section with two axes of symmetry, such as our rectangle, the centroid is also the shear centre (strižno središče), the point through which a transverse force must pass so that the section does not rotate about the axis of the element during bending (explained in chapter 16). Torsion therefore causes no bending and bending causes no rotation of the section. The torque is proportional to the rotation of the section per unit length,

\[M_{\mathrm{x}} = G J\,\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}' , \tag{12.16}\]

where \(G\) is the shear modulus and \(J\) the torsion constant (torzijska konstanta) of the section, a number with the unit m\(^4\) that depends only on the shape of the section. We take the equation as an assumption of the model, as we took the axial force as \(N = EA\,\bar u'\). Equilibrium of a slice of the element is by equation (5.12) in the component \(x\) equal to \(M_{\mathrm{x}}' + m_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) (\(m_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the distributed torque per unit length), which has the same form as \(N' + q_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) for the axial force. Without a distributed torque \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) is constant along the element and the rotation \(\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\) is linear.

We take the value of \(J\) for our strip \(20 \times 40\) mm as data and do not compute it. The computation needs the shear stresses in a section that warps and is in chapter 16. SADD (9.5.12) (PDF p. 264) gives for a rectangular section with sides \(2a\) and \(2b\), \(a < b\), the torque \(T = G\,\alpha\,J\) with the rotation \(\alpha\) per unit length, in which \(J\) is the series

\[J = \frac{16\,a^3 b}{3} - \frac{1024\,a^4}{\pi^5}\sum_{\mathrm{n} = 1, 3, 5, \dots}\frac{1}{n^5}\tanh\frac{n\pi b}{2a} , \tag{12.17}\]

where SADD writes the shear modulus as \(\mu\) (its \(\mu\) is our \(G\)) and we have taken \(G\,\alpha\) out. Beware that SADD in (9.3.23) calls the product \(G J\) by the symbol \(J\), while we use \(J\) for the geometric part only. For \(a = 10\) mm and \(b = 20\) mm the first term is \(106\,667\) mm\(^4\) and the terms of the series are \(0{,}99627\), \(0{,}00412\), \(0{,}00032\), ..., hence

\[J = 73\,178\ \text{mm}^4 = 7{,}3178\cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{m}^4 , \qquad G J = 75{,}385\ \text{GPa}\cdot J = 5516{,}5\ \text{N m}^2 .\]

No claim of this section depends on how \(J\) is computed: in all of them \(J\) is a constant positive number. Why we do not simply take the polar moment of inertia \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = \int(\bar y^2 + \bar z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A = 133\,333\) mm\(^4\) is shown by the computation at the end of the section. A rectangular section bulges out of its plane in torsion (SADD (9.5.14) and figure 9.13, PDF p. 265), hence \(J = 0{,}549\,I_{\mathrm{p}}\).

The model has one more idealization that we must name. The clamp at \(A\) and the rigid node at \(B\) do not prevent the warping of the section. A real clamp would prevent it and the column would be slightly stiffer than our model shows. For an I-beam five times as long as it is deep, COOK (PDF pp. 42-43) states that complete restraint of warping at the clamp reduces the rotation of the end by about half. How much it would reduce the rotation of our column, this section does not measure.

How do we write the rotation of a section in space? In the plane the rotation was one number, \(\varphi = v'\). In space the section moves as a rigid body (by assumption the section does not deform). A small motion without deformation has by theorem 1.134 the form \(\vek u(P) = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) with a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) (this is the small rotation tensor, definition 1.116). An antisymmetric \(3 \times 3\) matrix has three independent elements. Let us write them as

\[\begin{aligned} \mat W &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\varphi_{\mathrm{z}} & \varphi_{\mathrm{y}} \\ \varphi_{\mathrm{z}} & 0 & -\varphi_{\mathrm{x}} \\ -\varphi_{\mathrm{y}} & \varphi_{\mathrm{x}} & 0 \end{bmatrix} , \\ &\qquad \text{so} \qquad \mat W\,\vek b = \vek\varphi\times\vek b \ \text{ for every vector } \vek b , \end{aligned} \tag{12.18}\]

where \(\vek\varphi = (\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{y}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{z}})\) is the rotation vector (vektor zasuka) and the vector product is the one of definition 2.30 (the left and right sides are equal component by component). The component \(\varphi_{\mathrm{z}}\) is the rotation about the axis \(z\) counterclockwise, seen from the tip of the axis, and in the plane case it is the rotation \(\varphi\) of section 12.4. Thus \(-\varphi_{\mathrm{z}} = W_{\mathrm{xy}} = \omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\), as in step 4 of the proof of lemma 12.18.

How is the rotation \(\vek\varphi\) related to the derivatives \(v'\) and \(w'\)? Before loading the axis of the element has the direction \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), after loading the tangent \((1 + u', v', w')\), which for small slopes is in a first approximation \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + (0, v', w')\). The section is perpendicular to the axis and turns with it, so the difference is \(\vek\varphi\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = (0, \varphi_{\mathrm{z}}, -\varphi_{\mathrm{y}})\). Hence

\[\varphi_{\mathrm{z}} = v' , \qquad \varphi_{\mathrm{y}} = -w' . \tag{12.19}\]

We check the sign of \(\varphi_{\mathrm{y}}\) on the strain as well. A point of the section at distances \(y\) and \(z\) from the centroid moves after the rigid rotation in the direction of the axis \(x\) by \((\vek\varphi\times\vek r)_{\mathrm{x}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{y}}\,z - \varphi_{\mathrm{z}}\,y = -w'\,z - v'\,y\), so

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = u' - y\,v'' - z\,w'' . \tag{12.20}\]

The moment about the axis \(y\) is by definition \(M_{\mathrm{y}} = \int z\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}A = -E I_{\mathrm{y}}\,w''\) (the vector product \(\vek r\times\vek t\) has the component \(y\) equal to \(z\,t_{\mathrm{x}} - x\,t_{\mathrm{z}}\)), which is the equation of section 5.14.5.

Definition 12.21 Space frame element (element prostorskega okvirja)

A space frame (prostorski okvir) is a model of a structure of straight beams in space that are connected in rigid nodes: at a node the ends of all elements have the same displacement \((u, v, w)\) and the same rotation vector \(\vek\varphi\) (equation (12.18)), as for the plane frame (definition 5.90). Let the element be a straight beam with nodes 1 and 2, length \(h\), axis through the centroids of the sections, right-handed local axes \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\), \(\bar z\) (the axis \(\bar x\) from 1 to 2, \(\bar y\) and \(\bar z\) the principal axes of the section) and constant \(EA\), \(EI_{\mathrm{y}} = E\int\bar z^2\,\mathrm{d}A\), \(EI_{\mathrm{z}} = E\int\bar y^2\,\mathrm{d}A\) and \(GJ\). The space frame element (element prostorskega okvirja) is this element together with a column of twelve real numbers, the local nodal displacements,

\[\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} = (\bar u_1,\ \bar v_1,\ \bar w_1,\ \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}1},\ \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{y}1},\ \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{z}1},\ \bar u_2,\ \bar v_2,\ \bar w_2,\ \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}2},\ \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{y}2},\ \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{z}2})^\T ,\]

that is, the displacement and the rotation vector of each node in local axes, and with the fields along the axis: the axial displacement \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}\) and the rotation \(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{xh}}\) are linear (shape functions of definition 7.2), the transverse displacements are Hermite (definition 12.1), \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\,(\bar v_1, \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{z}1}, \bar v_2, \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{z}2})^\T\) and \(\bar w_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\,(\bar w_1, -\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{y}1}, \bar w_2, -\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{y}2})^\T\), because by equation (12.19) \(\bar w' = -\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{y}}\). In the global axes \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\) the element has a column \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) of twelve numbers in the same order.

Source: COOK §2.3 (PDF pp. 41-43: element with twelve unknowns, torsional stiffness \(GK/L\), the model holds for two axes of symmetry and free warping), GR §5.3.4 (PDF pp. 404-405: principal bending axes and free warping, rotations \(\psi_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{z}}\) tied to the displacements by (5.149)). ONATE2 §4.4 (PDF pp. 211-216) has for the space beam an element of Timoshenko type with reduced integration, so we do not cite it here for the matrix. The notation and the sign \(\varphi_{\mathrm{y}} = -w'\) are ours, derived in the text before the definition (COOK PDF p. 42 only mentions sign differences caused by the directions of the rotations).

Figure 12.15 shows the twelve unknowns of the element. Each of the two nodes has three displacements (left) and three components of the rotation vector (right). The rotation vector is drawn as an arrow with two heads along the axis about which it rotates, in the sense of the right-handed screw, like the moments in figure 5.85.

12.5.2 The element matrix

We obtain the element matrix from energy, as for the frame element. The energy of the element is a sum of four parts, each containing its own unknowns: axial, torsional and two bending parts. The matrix is therefore assembled from four blocks and has no other terms.

Lemma 12.22 Stiffness matrix of a space frame element (togostna matrika elementa prostorskega okvirja)

Let a space frame element (definition 12.21) have length \(h\) and no load along it, and let \(\mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\) be the Hermite row of definition 12.3. Then the strain energy of the element is \(U_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12\,\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) and the forces and moments that the surroundings exert on the nodes of the element, in local components (per node a force \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\), \(\bar z\) and a moment about \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\), \(\bar z\)), are \(\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{e}} = \bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\), where \(\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\) is a symmetric \(12 \times 12\) matrix with four blocks and zeros elsewhere. If we number the unknowns from 1 to 12 in the order of the definition, the blocks are:

  1. axial, on the unknowns \((\bar u_1, \bar u_2)\) (numbers 1 and 7): \(\dfrac{EA}{h}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\),
  2. torsional, on \((\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}1}, \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}2})\) (numbers 4 and 10): \(\dfrac{GJ}{h}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\),
  3. bending in the plane \(\bar x\bar y\), on \((\bar v_1, \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{z}1}, \bar v_2, \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{z}2})\) (numbers 2, 6, 8, 12): the matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) of lemma 12.4 with \(EI_{\mathrm{z}}\),
  4. bending in the plane \(\bar x\bar z\), on \((\bar w_1, \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{y}1}, \bar w_2, \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{y}2})\) (numbers 3, 5, 9, 11):
    \[\begin{aligned} \mat T\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat T &= \frac{EI_{\mathrm{y}}}{h^3}\begin{bmatrix} 12 & -6h & -12 & -6h \\ -6h & 4h^2 & 6h & 2h^2 \\ -12 & 6h & 12 & 6h \\ -6h & 2h^2 & 6h & 4h^2 \end{bmatrix} , \\ &\qquad \mat T = \mathrm{diag}(1, -1, 1, -1) , \end{aligned} \tag{12.21}\]
    where \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the beam element matrix with \(EI_{\mathrm{y}}\).
Proof

We have to show that the energy is a sum of four quadratic forms in separate groups of unknowns (hence the zeros outside the blocks) and that the forces of the surroundings equal \(\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) in each block.

  1. The axis passes through the centroid and the axes \(\bar y\), \(\bar z\) are principal, so \(\int\bar y\,\mathrm{d}A = \int\bar z\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\) and \(\int\bar y\bar z\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\) (corollary 5.31). With \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E(\bar u' - \bar y\,\bar v'' - \bar z\,\bar w'')\) from equation (12.20) we therefore have \(\tfrac12\int E(\bar u' - \bar y\,\bar v'' - \bar z\,\bar w'')^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \tfrac12\big(EA\,\bar u'^2 + EI_{\mathrm{z}}\,\bar v''^2 + EI_{\mathrm{y}}\,\bar w''^2\big)\): the mixed terms are products with three sums that are zero (as in the proof of lemma 5.33 for one plane).
  2. The torsional energy per unit length is the work of the moment \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) on the rotation \(\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}'\) of the section with the relation (12.16), that is \(\tfrac12\,GJ\,\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}'^2\). By the assumption of the model (the centroid is the shear centre) torsion is not coupled to bending, so the energies add. The energy of the element is \(U_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12\int_0^h\big(EA\,\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}'^2 + GJ\,\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{xh}}'^2 + EI_{\mathrm{z}}\,\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}''^2 + EI_{\mathrm{y}}\,\bar w_{\mathrm{h}}''^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}\bar x\).
  3. Each of the four terms contains only its own group of unknowns (axial \(\bar u_1\), \(\bar u_2\), torsional \(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}1}\), \(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}2}\), the bending ones four each). A quadratic form in separate groups has all matrix entries between the groups equal to zero, so the matrix is assembled from four blocks and is symmetric.
  4. Axial block: \(\tfrac12\int_0^h EA\,\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}'^2\,\mathrm{d}\bar x = \tfrac12\,\tfrac{EA}{h}(\bar u_2 - \bar u_1)^2\) (lemma 7.5, point 2). Torsional block: since \(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{xh}}' = (\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}2} - \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}1})/h\) is constant, \(\tfrac12\int_0^h GJ\,\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{xh}}'^2\,\mathrm{d}\bar x = \tfrac12\,\tfrac{GJ}{h}(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}2} - \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}1})^2\), the same computation under another name.
  5. Bending block in the plane \(\bar x\bar y\): \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{y}}\) with \(\vek d_{\mathrm{y}} = (\bar v_1, \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{z}1}, \bar v_2, \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{z}2})^\T\), so by lemma 12.4 (point 1) the energy is \(\tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{y}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{y}}\) with \(EI_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  6. Bending block in the plane \(\bar x\bar z\): \(\bar w_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat T\,\vek d_{\mathrm{z}}\) with \(\vek d_{\mathrm{z}} = (\bar w_1, \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{y}1}, \bar w_2, \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{y}2})^\T\), because \(\bar w' = -\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{y}}\) (definition 12.21). By lemma 12.4 the energy is \(\tfrac12\,(\mat T\,\vek d_{\mathrm{z}})^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,(\mat T\,\vek d_{\mathrm{z}}) = \tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{z}}^\T(\mat T\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat T)\,\vek d_{\mathrm{z}}\), because \(\mat T\) is symmetric. The product \(\mat T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\mat T\) changes the sign of the entries in which exactly one of the indices is 2 or 4. This gives equation (12.21).
  7. Forces of the surroundings. The work of the forces of the surroundings on a rigid section for a virtual displacement \(\delta\vek a\) and rotation \(\delta\vek\varphi\) is \(\int\vek t\cdot(\delta\vek a + \delta\vek\varphi\times\vek r)\,\mathrm{d}A = \vek F\cdot\delta\vek a + \delta\vek\varphi\cdot\int\vek r\times\vek t\,\mathrm{d}A = \vek F\cdot\delta\vek a + \vek M\cdot\delta\vek\varphi\) (cyclic exchange in the mixed product, lemma 2.51, point 1). The forces belonging to the unknowns \((u, v, w, \varphi_{\mathrm{x}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{y}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{z}})\) are therefore the components of the force and the moment in this order, at the start of the element \(-\vek F(0)\) and \(-\vek M(0)\), at the end \(\vek F(h)\) and \(\vek M(h)\) (definition of the internal force, section 5.2.1).
  8. Axial forces and torques: the axial force is given by lemma 7.5 (point 3), the torque is by equation (5.12) and \(m_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) constant, \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = GJ(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}2} - \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}1})/h\), so the force of the surroundings on node 1 is \(-M_{\mathrm{x}} = \tfrac{GJ}{h}(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}1} - \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}2})\) and on node 2 it is \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), which is the torsional block times \((\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}1}, \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}2})\).
  9. Bending in the plane \(\bar x\bar y\): the forces are \((-V_{\mathrm{y}}(0), -M_{\mathrm{z}}(0), V_{\mathrm{y}}(h), M_{\mathrm{z}}(h))\) with \(M_{\mathrm{z}} = EI_{\mathrm{z}}\,\bar v''\) and \(V_{\mathrm{y}} = -M_{\mathrm{z}}'\) (equations (5.12), \(m = 0\)), which is the plane \(V\), \(M\) of section 12.1, so \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{y}}\) by lemma 12.4 (point 2). Bending in the plane \(\bar x\bar z\): \(M_{\mathrm{y}} = -EI_{\mathrm{y}}\,\bar w''\) and from the component \(y\) of equation (5.12), \(M_{\mathrm{y}}' - V_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) (because \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek F = (0, -V_{\mathrm{z}}, V_{\mathrm{y}})\)), we get \(V_{\mathrm{z}} = M_{\mathrm{y}}' = -EI_{\mathrm{y}}\,\bar w'''\). Comparison with the plane \(V = -EI\,v'''\), \(M = EI\,v''\) shows that \(V_{\mathrm{z}}\) is like \(V\), while \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\) is the opposite of the moment \(M\) for \(v = \bar w\). The forces \((-V_{\mathrm{z}}(0), -M_{\mathrm{y}}(0), V_{\mathrm{z}}(h), M_{\mathrm{y}}(h))\) are therefore the plane forces of the field \(\bar w_{\mathrm{h}}\) with the second and fourth entries of opposite sign, so \(\mat T\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,(\mat T\,\vek d_{\mathrm{z}}) = (\mat T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\mat T)\,\vek d_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Source: COOK (2.3-8) (PDF p. 41, with a comment on signs on p. 42), GR (5.151) (PDF p. 405). The sources only state the matrix, COOK with different directions of the rotations. The proof, including the block ((12.21)) from the relation \(\varphi_{\mathrm{y}} = -w'\), is not from the sources.

The matrix consists of the bar and beam blocks that we already have and one block that is the same as the axial one. Torsion is thus as simple in the element matrix as the axial force: the torque is \(GJ/h\) times the difference of the rotations, as the axial force is \(EA/h\) times the difference of the displacements. In the L-frame both elements have \(h = 1\) m. The column \(AB\) has the local axes \(\bar y = X\) (width \(40\) mm) and \(\bar z = Y\) (thickness \(20\) mm) and therefore the weak moment of inertia \(I_{\mathrm{y}} = 26\,667\) mm\(^4\) about the axis \(\bar y\), which bends the column in the direction of the force \(Y\). The beam \(BC\) has \(\bar y = Y\) and \(\bar z = Z\), so in the plane \(\bar x\bar y\), in which it bends, also the weak moment of inertia \(I_{\mathrm{z}} = 26\,667\) mm\(^4\). The weak stiffness is \(EI_{\mathrm{w}} = 5226{,}67\) N m\(^2\). The coefficients of the block (12.21) of the column and of the block of the beam in the plane \(\bar x\bar y\) are therefore the same: \(12EI_{\mathrm{w}}/h^3 = 62\,720\) N/m, \(6EI_{\mathrm{w}}/h^2 = 31\,360\) N, \(4EI_{\mathrm{w}}/h = 20\,906{,}7\) N m, \(2EI_{\mathrm{w}}/h = 10\,453{,}3\) N m, and the torsional coefficient is \(GJ/h = 5516{,}5\) N m. The axial block \(EA/h = 1{,}568\cdot 10^8\) N/m does not affect the load in the direction \(Y\).

12.5.3 Turning the axes

We have the matrix \(\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\) in local axes. For assembly we need it in global ones. For the plane frame the axes were turned about \(z\) and the rotation of the node stayed the same number (lemma 12.18, step 4). In space the axes are turned arbitrarily and we do not yet know how the rotation of a node is mapped. We have to map three things: the displacement vector, the rotation vector and the moment, which is a vector product. The displacement and the force are mapped by the rotation matrix (lemma 2.38). The moment is a vector product of two vectors and the rotation comes from an antisymmetric matrix, so we need two more things: how the vector product is mapped and how the rotation is.

The vector product is defined by components in a right-handed system. When we turn the system by the rotation matrix \(\mat Q\), we compute it from the components in the new system. Do we obtain the same vector? We do, if the new system is right-handed. In a left-handed system we would have to multiply each component by \(-1\) (the section on the vector product in chapter 2).

Lemma 12.23 Turning the axes maps the rotation vector and the moment (zasuk osi preslika vektor zasuka in moment)

Let two right-handed orthogonal Cartesian systems with the same origin and the same unit of length be given, the old one with axes \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\) and the new one with axes \(\bar x\), \(\bar y\), \(\bar z\), and let \(\mat Q\) be the rotation matrix from the old to the new system (definition 2.37). Then:

  1. \(\det\mat Q = 1\) and for all vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) we have \(\mat Q\,(\vek a\times\vek b) = (\mat Q\,\vek a)\times(\mat Q\,\vek b)\).
  2. A small rigid displacement \(\vek u(P) = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) with an antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) and rotation vector \(\vek\varphi\) (equation (12.18)) has in the new system the form \(\bar{\vek u}(\bar P) = \bar{\vek a} + \bar{\mat W}\,\bar{\vek r}_{\mathrm{P}}\) with \(\bar{\vek a} = \mat Q\,\vek a\), the antisymmetric matrix \(\bar{\mat W} = \mat Q\,\mat W\,\mat Q^\T\) and the rotation vector \(\bar{\vek\varphi} = \mat Q\,\vek\varphi\).
  3. The moment \(\vek M = \int\vek r\times\vek t\,\mathrm{d}A\) of forces \(\vek t\) on a section has in the new system the components \(\bar{\vek M} = \mat Q\,\vek M\).

Hence for a space frame element with the local axes in the rows of the matrix \(\mat Q\) we have

\[\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} , \qquad \bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R\,\vek F_{\mathrm{e}} , \qquad \mat R = \mathrm{diag}(\mat Q, \mat Q, \mat Q, \mat Q) , \tag{12.22}\]

where \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\) are the displacements and the forces of the surroundings in global components, and \(\mat R\) is a \(12 \times 12\) matrix with four blocks \(\mat Q\).

Proof

We have to show that the mapping of the vector product, of the displacement and of the rotation is the same matrix \(\mat Q\).

  1. By the section on the determinant (chapter 2), by theorem 2.52 and lemma 2.51 (point 6) we have \((\det\mat Q)^2 = \det(\mat Q\,\mat Q^\T) = \det\mat I = 1\) (lemma 2.40). The rows of the matrix \(\mat Q\) are the components of the vectors \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}}\) in the old system (definition 2.37), so \(\det\mat Q = \det\mat Q^\T = \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\times\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}})\) by the definition of the determinant. This is the mixed product of a triple that is right-handed by assumption (definition 2.48), hence positive, and \(\det\mat Q = 1\).
  2. Let \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\) be arbitrary vectors. The matrix with the columns \(\mat Q\vek a\), \(\mat Q\vek b\), \(\mat Q\vek c\) is the product \(\mat Q\,[\vek a\ \vek b\ \vek c]\), so by theorem 2.52 \(\det(\mat Q\vek a, \mat Q\vek b, \mat Q\vek c) = \det\mat Q\,\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c) = \det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c)\).
  3. By the definition of the determinant and cyclic exchange (lemma 2.51, point 1) we have \(\det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek w) = \vek w\cdot(\vek u\times\vek v)\). So the left side of step 2 equals \(\mat Q\vek c\cdot(\mat Q\vek a\times\mat Q\vek b)\) and the right side \(\vek c\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b)\). The matrix \(\mat Q^\T\) is the inverse of the matrix \(\mat Q\) (lemma 2.40), so also \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\) and \(\mat Q\vek x\cdot\mat Q\vek y = \vek x\cdot\vek y\), hence \(\vek c\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b) = \mat Q\vek c\cdot\mat Q(\vek a\times\vek b)\). The difference \(\vek z = \mat Q(\vek a\times\vek b) - (\mat Q\vek a)\times(\mat Q\vek b)\) therefore has scalar product zero with \(\mat Q\vek c\) for every \(\vek c\). Since \(\mat Q\) is invertible, \(\mat Q\vek c\) is an arbitrary vector, so also \(\vek z\), and \(|\vek z|^2 = 0\) gives \(\vek z = \vek 0\). This is point 1.
  4. Point 2. The point \(P\) has in the new system the position vector \(\bar{\vek r}_{\mathrm{P}} = \mat Q\,\vek r_{\mathrm{P}}\) and the displacement \(\bar{\vek u} = \mat Q\,\vek u\) (lemma 2.38, point 1). By theorem 1.134 we have \(\vek r_{\mathrm{P}} = \mat Q^\T\bar{\vek r}_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(\bar{\vek u} = \mat Q\vek a + \mat Q\,\mat W\,\mat Q^\T\,\bar{\vek r}_{\mathrm{P}}\). The matrix \(\bar{\mat W} = \mat Q\mat W\mat Q^\T\) is antisymmetric, because \(\bar{\mat W}^\T = \mat Q\,\mat W^\T\mat Q^\T = -\bar{\mat W}\) (lemma 1.101).
  5. For every vector \(\bar{\vek b}\) we have by step 4 and equation (12.18) \(\bar{\mat W}\bar{\vek b} = \mat Q\,\mat W\,(\mat Q^\T\bar{\vek b}) = \mat Q\big(\vek\varphi\times\mat Q^\T\bar{\vek b}\big)\). By step 3 this is \((\mat Q\vek\varphi)\times(\mat Q\mat Q^\T\bar{\vek b}) = (\mat Q\vek\varphi)\times\bar{\vek b}\), because \(\mat Q\mat Q^\T = \mat I\). An antisymmetric matrix that equals \(\bar{\vek b}\mapsto\vek w\times\bar{\vek b}\) for every \(\bar{\vek b}\) has elements determined by \(\vek w\) (we insert \(\bar{\vek b} = \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}, \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}, \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}}\)), so the rotation vector of the matrix \(\bar{\mat W}\) equals \(\mat Q\vek\varphi\).
  6. Point 3. The force \(\vek t\) and the position vector \(\vek r\) have in the new system the components \(\mat Q\vek t\) and \(\mat Q\vek r\) (lemma 2.38), so by point 1 we have \(\int(\mat Q\vek r)\times(\mat Q\vek t)\,\mathrm{d}A = \mat Q\int\vek r\times\vek t\,\mathrm{d}A\), because \(\mat Q\) can be taken out of the integral (the integral is linear, lemma 3.39).
  7. The element. The displacement and the rotation vector of a node are mapped by point 2 with \(\mat Q\) each, so \(\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) with four blocks \(\mat Q\) (two for each node). The force and the moment of the surroundings are mapped by lemma 2.38 and point 3 with \(\mat Q\), so \(\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R\,\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The sources state the mapping of turned axes for displacements and nodal rotations, without a proof for the rotation vector: COOK (2.4-8), (2.4-9) (PDF p. 46, displacements and rotations are mapped in the same way), GR (5.160)-(5.163) (PDF pp. 407-408). ONATE2 (4.85), (4.86) (PDF p. 216) map the stiffness matrix with the same orthogonal matrices.

The lemma says that the rotation behaves like the displacement, so the matrix \(\mat R\) is the same as for the plane, only with one block \(\mat Q\) for each vector. The plane case is a special case: for a rotation about \(z\) we have \(\vek\varphi = (0, 0, \varphi)\) and \(\mat Q\vek\varphi = \vek\varphi\), which is the statement that the rotation \(\varphi\) does not change when turned about \(z\) (lemma 12.18, step 4). Since energy and work are scalars, \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\cdot\delta\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{e}}\cdot\delta\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\), and as for the plane frame it follows from \(\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{e}} = \bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) that \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R^\T\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat R\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) (\(\mat R^\T\) is the inverse of \(\mat R\) by lemma 2.40). The element matrix in global axes is

\[\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R^\T\,\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat R , \qquad \vek f_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R^\T\bar{\vek f}_{\mathrm{e}} . \tag{12.23}\]

The matrix is symmetric and has the energy \(U_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) as for the plane element.

12.5.4 Assembly and accuracy

Is the solution of the assembled system again a solution of the space frame? We showed this for the plane frame (theorem 12.20). The solution of the space frame (rešitev prostorskega okvirja) for a given load is a set of fields \(\bar u\), \(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar v\), \(\bar w\) on the elements, with \(N = EA\,\bar u'\), \(M_{\mathrm{x}} = GJ\,\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}'\), \(M_{\mathrm{z}} = EI_{\mathrm{z}}\,\bar v''\), \(M_{\mathrm{y}} = -EI_{\mathrm{y}}\,\bar w''\) and \(V_{\mathrm{y}} = -M_{\mathrm{z}}'\), \(V_{\mathrm{z}} = M_{\mathrm{y}}'\), for which the following holds:

  1. On each element \(N' = -\bar q_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(V_{\mathrm{y}}' = -\bar q_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(V_{\mathrm{z}}' = -\bar q_{\mathrm{z}}\) (equation (5.12), force components) with continuous loads \(\bar q_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar q_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\bar q_{\mathrm{z}}\) in local axes, and \(M_{\mathrm{x}}' = 0\) (no distributed torque).
  2. At each node all elements have the same displacement and the same rotation vector.
  3. At each node the joint is in equilibrium with the external force \(\vek F_{\mathrm{J}}\) and the external moment \(\vek M_{\mathrm{J}}\) (vectors).
  4. The supports prevent the corresponding components of displacement or rotation and the reactions act only in these directions.
Corollary 12.24 Finite element method for a space frame (metoda končnih elementov za prostorski okvir)

Let a connected space frame (definition 12.21, from each node we reach every other node along elements) be divided into space frame elements with constant \(EA\), \(EI_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(EI_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(GJ\) on each element, with loads at the nodes (force and moment as vectors), with continuous axial and transverse loads on the elements without a distributed torque and with supports at the nodes. Let the only small rigid displacement of the frame in which the prevented components are zero be the zero one. Let \(\mat K\) and \(\vek f\) be the matrix and the right-hand side of theorem 7.13 with the matrices \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) and forces \(\vek f_{\mathrm{e}}\) of equation (12.23) (consistent forces \(\bar{\vek f}_{\mathrm{e}}\) by definition 12.6 in both bending planes, in the plane \(\bar x\bar z\) with the sign changed at the rotations because of \(\bar w' = -\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{y}}\)) and let \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} - \vek f_{\mathrm{e}}\). Then:

  1. The rows of the system \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f\) for the free unknowns of the node \(J\) are the joint equilibrium: \(\sum_{\mathrm{e} \ni \mathrm{J}}\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}^{(J)} = \vek P_{\mathrm{J}}\), where \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}^{(J)}\) are the six components of the forces of the surroundings on the element \(e\) at the node \(J\) (three forces and three moments) and \(\vek P_{\mathrm{J}}\) is the external force and external moment of the node \(J\) (\(\vek F_{\mathrm{J}}\) and \(\vek M_{\mathrm{J}}\) of condition 3).
  2. The reduced system (theorem 7.18) has exactly one solution \(\vek d\).
  3. The displacements and rotation vectors of the nodes of this solution are exactly the displacements and rotation vectors of the solution of the frame, and \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\) are the forces and moments that the surroundings exert on the nodes of the element. If there is no load on the elements, the fields \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}\), \(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{xh}}\), \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}\), \(\bar w_{\mathrm{h}}\) are exact along the whole length.
Proof

We have to show that the rows of the system give the equilibrium of the joints (point 1), that the matrix of the free unknowns is positive definite (point 2) and that with a correction of the fields we obtain a solution of the frame, which is unique (point 3). The steps follow the proof of theorem 12.20.

  1. By point 1 of theorem 7.13 the row \(I\) equals \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}}(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} - \vek f_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{i}} = P_{\mathrm{I}}\), where \(P_{\mathrm{I}}\) is the component of the external force or moment of the node in the direction of the unknown \(I\). This is \(\sum_{\mathrm{e} \ni \mathrm{J}}\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}^{(J)} = \vek P_{\mathrm{J}}\), component by component.
  2. The force and the moment of the surroundings on the element are by lemma 12.23 in global components \(\mat R^\T\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\), as in equation (12.23). The piece of the frame around the node \(J\) is in equilibrium of forces and moments, and steps 1 to 4 of the proof of lemma 5.91 hold for all three components of the moment, because the moment equilibrium (2.35) is a vector equation. The element acts on the piece with a force and a moment opposite to \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\) (as in step 4 of the proof of lemma 12.19), so equilibrium of the piece gives the same joint equilibrium as in step 1, which is the joint equilibrium that condition 3 of the solution of the frame requires.
  3. Point 2. Let \(\vek d\) have the prescribed unknowns equal to zero and \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = 0\). By point 2 of theorem 7.13 \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\), each term is \(2U_{\mathrm{e}} \ge 0\) (lemma 12.22, the matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R^\T\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\mat R\) is symmetric, so the hypothesis of corollary 7.14 holds for \(\mat K\)), hence \(U_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\) for each element. The energy is a sum of four nonnegative parts, so \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}' = 0\), \(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{xh}}' = 0\), \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}'' = 0\) and \(\bar w_{\mathrm{h}}'' = 0\) (as in step 6 of the proof of lemma 12.19): \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}\) and \(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{xh}}\) are constant, \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}\) and \(\bar w_{\mathrm{h}}\) linear.
  4. Such a field is a rigid body motion. A point of the axis at \(\bar x\) moves by \(\big(\bar u_0,\ \bar v_0 + \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{z}}\,\bar x,\ \bar w_0 - \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{y}}\,\bar x\big) = \bar{\vek a} + \vek\varphi\times\bar x\,\vek e_{\bar{x}}\) with a constant \(\vek\varphi = (\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}, \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{y}}, \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{z}})\) (\(\vek\varphi\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = (0, \varphi_{\mathrm{z}}, -\varphi_{\mathrm{y}})\), equation (12.19)), which is a field of the form \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) of theorem 1.134. Two elements at a common node have the same displacement and the same rotation vector (lemma 12.23, point 2, for rotations in global axes), and such a field is determined by the displacement of one point and the rotation vector, so the connected frame moves as one whole, that is, as a small rigid displacement of the frame, which is zero by assumption because of the supports. Hence \(\vek d = \vek 0\), and by theorem 7.18 the matrix of the free unknowns is positive definite and the system has exactly one solution.
  5. Point 3. Let \(\vek d\) be this solution and \(\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\). For each element let \(\bar u = \bar u_{\mathrm{h}} + \bar u_0\), \(\bar v = \bar v_{\mathrm{h}} + \bar v_0\), \(\bar w = \bar w_{\mathrm{h}} + \bar w_0\), \(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}} = \bar\varphi_{\mathrm{xh}}\), where \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}\), \(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{xh}}\), \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}\), \(\bar w_{\mathrm{h}}\) are the finite element fields, \(\bar u_0\) is the solution of the equation \(EA\,\bar u_0'' = -\bar q_{\mathrm{x}}\) with zero values at the ends, \(\bar v_0\) the solution of the equation \(EI_{\mathrm{z}}\,\bar v_0'''' = \bar q_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\bar w_0\) the solution of the equation \(EI_{\mathrm{y}}\,\bar w_0'''' = \bar q_{\mathrm{z}}\), both with zero values and slopes at the ends. Such functions exist and are unique (theorem 5.45, as in step 3 of the proof of theorem 12.20). Without load \(\bar u_0 = \bar v_0 = \bar w_0 = 0\).
  6. The fields \(\bar u\), \(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar v\), \(\bar w\) satisfy conditions 1 and 2 of the solution of the space frame. Condition 1: \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}'' = 0\), \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}'''' = 0\), \(\bar w_{\mathrm{h}}'''' = 0\) (a linear and a cubic function), so for example \(V_{\mathrm{y}}' = -M_{\mathrm{z}}'' = -EI_{\mathrm{z}}\,\bar v'''' = -EI_{\mathrm{z}}\,\bar v_0'''' = -\bar q_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{z}}' = M_{\mathrm{y}}'' = -EI_{\mathrm{y}}\,\bar w'''' = -\bar q_{\mathrm{z}}\), and the torque is constant. Condition 2: \(\bar u_0\), \(\bar v_0\), \(\bar w_0\) are zero at the ends of the element with zero slope, so the fields have at the ends the same displacements and rotations as the finite element fields, these are the values of \(\vek d\), which are equal for elements at the same node.
  7. Forces of the surroundings. For the axial, the torsional and both bending planes separately, the force of the surroundings is the sum of the forces of the finite element fields and the forces of the corrections \(\bar u_0\), \(\bar v_0\), \(\bar w_0\). The first are \(\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) (lemma 12.22), because the element has no load, the second are by step 6 of the proof of theorem 12.20 and corollary 12.15 \(-\bar{\vek f}_{\mathrm{e}}\) (in the plane \(\bar x\bar z\) with the same changed sign). The sum is \(\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} - \bar{\vek f}_{\mathrm{e}}\), and by equation (12.23) this is in global components \(\vek F_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  8. By point 1 and step 7 equilibrium holds at the nodes, so condition 3 of the solution. Condition 4 is satisfied by \(\vek d\) by construction. The fields \(\bar u\), \(\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar v\), \(\bar w\) are therefore a solution of the space frame. It is the only one. The difference of two solutions has no loads. For each element, by theorem 5.62 for \(\bar v\) and for \(\bar w\) (the plane version with \(\bar w\) in place of \(\bar v\), because of \(M_{\mathrm{y}} = -EI_{\mathrm{y}}\,\bar w''\) with the boundary term \(V_{\mathrm{z}}\,\delta\bar w + M_{\mathrm{y}}\,\delta\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{y}}\)) and by integration by parts for the axial force and the torque, the virtual work equals the boundary terms \(\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{e}}\cdot\delta\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) (step 7 of the proof of lemma 12.22). Over the nodes these terms add up to the work of the external load as in step 4 of the proof of lemma 12.19, with the joint equilibrium of step 2, and the reactions do no work. With the virtual displacement equal to the difference and a zero right-hand side we obtain \(\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\int_0^{h_{\mathrm{e}}}\big(EA\,\bar u'^2 + GJ\,\bar\varphi_{\mathrm{x}}'^2 + EI_{\mathrm{z}}\,\bar v''^2 + EI_{\mathrm{y}}\,\bar w''^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}\bar x = 0\). As in steps 3 and 4 the difference is a rigid displacement of the frame, which is zero by assumption.

Source: COOK §2.5 (PDF p. 47, each node is a small connector in equilibrium), ONATE2 (PDF pp. 49-50, exact nodal values for a plane beam). For the space frame the sources do not prove the accuracy. The proof is not from a source. Its basis is theorem 12.20.

The corollary has the same condition as the theorem for the plane frame: constant \(EI\) on the element and consistent forces for the load on the element. For a load only at the nodes the field is exact along the whole length, for a load on the element the displacements and rotations of the nodes and the forces at the ends are exact.
