Torsion has no load on the element, so its part is always exact, and as for the plane frame the accuracy depends on the model: the solution of the model with uniform torsion is exact, but not the solution of the spatial body.

12.5.5 The L-frame in space

Let us return to the question of the section. The L-frame of section 5.14.5, the column \(AB\) (\(a = 1\) m) along the axis \(Z\) and the beam \(BC\) (\(b = 1\) m) along the axis \(X\), is clamped at \(A\) and has at \(C\) the force \(F\) in the direction of the axis \(Y\). The points are \(A = (0, 0, 0)\), \(B = (0, 0, 1)\) and \(C = (1, 0, 1)\) m, the strip section is \(20 \times 40\) mm with axial \(EA = 1{,}568\cdot 10^8\) N, \(EI = 20\,906{,}7\) N m\(^2\) (about the strong axis), \(EI_{\mathrm{w}} = 5226{,}67\) N m\(^2\) (about the weak one), \(G = 75{,}385\) GPa and \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\) from equation (12.17). The strip stands so that in the plane of the frame \(XZ\) it is strong (\(40\) mm) and out of the plane weak (\(20\) mm).

The local axes of the column are \(\bar x = \vek e_{\mathrm{Z}}\), \(\bar y = \vek e_{\mathrm{X}}\), \(\bar z = \vek e_{\mathrm{Y}}\), so \(\mat Q_{\mathrm{AB}}\) has the rows \((0, 0, 1)\), \((1, 0, 0)\), \((0, 1, 0)\). The triple is right-handed: \(\bar x\times\bar y = \vek e_{\mathrm{Z}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{X}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{Y}} = \bar z\), and \(\det\mat Q_{\mathrm{AB}} = 1\) (computation in NumPy). The beam has the local axes \(\bar x = \vek e_{\mathrm{X}}\), \(\bar y = \vek e_{\mathrm{Y}}\), \(\bar z = \vek e_{\mathrm{Z}}\), so \(\mat Q_{\mathrm{BC}} = \mat I\). Each node has six unknowns \((u, v, w, \varphi_{\mathrm{X}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{Y}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{Z}})\), \(18\) in all, the clamp at \(A\) removes \(6\) of them, so \(12\) are free. Let us see which of these are nonzero. The elements lie along the axes \(Z\) and \(X\), so the block of the element matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R^\T\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\mat R\) couples the displacement \(v\) only with the rotations \(\varphi_{\mathrm{X}}\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{Z}}\) (bending out of the plane \(XZ\) and torsion), and the displacements \(u\), \(w\) only with the rotation \(\varphi_{\mathrm{Y}}\) (axial force and bending in the plane \(XZ\)). The group \((v, \varphi_{\mathrm{X}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{Z}})\) of the nodes \(B\) and \(C\) therefore has in the matrix \(\mat K\) all entries towards the other six free unknowns equal to zero (NumPy confirms that the largest absolute entry between the groups is \(0\)), the load \(F\) is in the first group, so the other six unknowns are zero (the reduced system has one solution by corollary 12.24). What remains is a \(6 \times 6\) system for \(\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} = (v_{\mathrm{B}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{X},\mathrm{B}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{B}}, v_{\mathrm{C}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{X},\mathrm{C}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{C}})\):

\[\begin{aligned} &\begin{bmatrix} 125\,440 & 31\,360 & 31\,360 & -62\,720 & 0 & 31\,360 \\ 31\,360 & 26\,423{,}2 & 0 & 0 & -5516{,}5 & 0 \\ 31\,360 & 0 & 26\,423{,}2 & -31\,360 & 0 & 10\,453{,}3 \\ -62\,720 & 0 & -31\,360 & 62\,720 & 0 & -31\,360 \\ 0 & -5516{,}5 & 0 & 0 & 5516{,}5 & 0 \\ 31\,360 & 0 & 10\,453{,}3 & -31\,360 & 0 & 20\,906{,}7 \end{bmatrix}\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} \\ &\qquad = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ F \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} . \end{aligned} \tag{12.24}\]

The units are N/m, N and N m by rows and columns, as fits the unknowns. Let us explain some entries. The displacement \(v_{\mathrm{B}}\) is for the column the displacement of the end (node 2), for the beam the displacement of the start (node 1), each of them contributes \(12EI_{\mathrm{w}}/h^3 = 62\,720\) N/m, so the entry \((1, 1)\) equals \(125\,440\) N/m. The rotation \(\varphi_{\mathrm{X},\mathrm{B}}\) is for the column a bending rotation (the entry \(4EI_{\mathrm{w}}/h = 20\,906{,}7\) N m), for the beam a torsional one (the entry \(GJ/h = 5516{,}5\) N m), together \(26\,423{,}2\) N m. The rotation \(\varphi_{\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{B}}\) is the other way round: torsional for the column, bending for the beam. The entry \((5, 5) = GJ/h\) is the torsion of the beam, because \(\varphi_{\mathrm{X},\mathrm{C}}\) is the rotation of the end of the beam about its axis.

For \(F = 50\) N the solution of the system (NumPy) gives

\[\begin{aligned} v_{\mathrm{B}} &= 3{,}189\ \text{mm} , & v_{\mathrm{C}} &= 15{,}441\ \text{mm} , & \varphi_{\mathrm{X},\mathrm{B}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{X},\mathrm{C}} &= -4{,}783\cdot 10^{-3} , \\ \varphi_{\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{B}} &= 9{,}064\cdot 10^{-3} , & \varphi_{\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{C}} &= 13{,}847\cdot 10^{-3} . \end{aligned}\]

The point \(C\) therefore moves by \(15{,}44\) mm in the direction of the force. Why at \(50\) N and not at \(500\) N, as in section 5.14.5? Statics holds at every size of the force and the internal forces are proportional to \(F\). The displacements, however, are a computation of the linear model, which requires small slopes, \(v'^2 \le 10^{-2}\) (section 5.3.3). At \(500\) N the model would give \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = 154{,}4\) mm, \(15\) % of the length of the element, and the slope \(\varphi_{\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{C}} = 0{,}138\), so \(\varphi^2 = 0{,}019\), beyond the limit. At \(50\) N we have \(\varphi_{\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{C}}^2 = 1{,}9\cdot 10^{-4}\).

We check the result in three ways. The first is each of the numbers in the system. The rotation of the column about the axis \(X\) is the rotation of a bending cantilever with the force \(F\) at the top, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{X},\mathrm{B}} = -F\,a^2/(2EI_{\mathrm{w}}) = -4{,}783\cdot 10^{-3}\), and since the torque of the beam is zero (the force \(F\) passes through its axis), the beam does not twist and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{X},\mathrm{C}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{X},\mathrm{B}}\). The rotation \(\varphi_{\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{B}} = F\,b\,a/(GJ) = 9{,}064\cdot 10^{-3}\) is the twisting of the column with the constant torque \(F\,b\) (by equation (12.16)). The displacement \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\) is the sum of three parts: the bending of the column \(v_{\mathrm{B}} = F\,a^3/(3EI_{\mathrm{w}}) = 3{,}1888\) mm, the rotation \(\varphi_{\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{B}}\) of the lever arm \(b\), that is the twisting of the column, \(b\,\varphi_{\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{B}} = F\,b^2\,a/(GJ) = 9{,}0637\) mm, and the bending of the beam \(F\,b^3/(3EI_{\mathrm{w}}) = 3{,}1888\) mm. The sum is \(15{,}4413\) mm, which is the result of the system.

The second way is by energy. The work of the force is by Clapeyron's theorem (theorem 4.86) \(\tfrac12\,F\,v_{\mathrm{C}} = 0{,}38603\) J, and the strain energy of the elements from their fields is \(0{,}22659\) J (torsion of the column) \(+\ 0{,}07972\) J (bending of the column) \(+\ 0{,}07972\) J (bending of the beam) \(= 0{,}38603\) J. Torsion carries \(58{,}7\) % of the energy and \(58{,}7\) % of the displacement. The sum \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = F\big(b^2 a/(GJ) + a^3/(3EI_{\mathrm{w}}) + b^3/(3EI_{\mathrm{w}})\big)\) uses only the internal forces from statics and the formulas for the cantilever and for torsion, so it is independent of the finite element method, and it agrees with it in all the digits.

The third way shows why we need \(J\). If instead of \(J\) we took the polar moment \(I_{\mathrm{p}} = 133\,333\) mm\(^4\), the twisting would be \(F\,b^2\,a/(G\,I_{\mathrm{p}}) = 4{,}97\) mm instead of \(9{,}06\) mm and \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = 11{,}35\) mm instead of \(15{,}44\) mm, which is \(26\) % too little (figure 12.16). A frame that twists therefore needs a property of the section that is not a moment of inertia. This is the torsion constant \(J\), which we compute in chapter 16.

The internal forces at \(F = 500\) N we obtain from the forces at the ends of the elements, \(\bar{\vek F}_{\mathrm{e}} = \bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) with \(\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat R\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\): at the start of the element the internal forces are \(-\bar{\vek F}\) of the first half of the column, at the end the second half (lemma 12.22, step 7). We obtain (NumPy, local components \(N\), \(V_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(V_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{z}}\)):

element \(N\) (N) \(V_{\mathrm{y}}\) (N) \(V_{\mathrm{z}}\) (N) \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) (\(\text{N m}\)) \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\) (\(\text{N m}\)) \(M_{\mathrm{z}}\) (\(\text{N m}\))
beam \(BC\), \(\bar x = 0\) \(0\) \(500\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\) \(500\)
column \(AB\), \(\bar x = a\) (below the node) \(0\) \(0\) \(500\) \(500\) \(0\) \(0\)
column \(AB\), \(\bar x = 0\) (clamp) \(0\) \(0\) \(500\) \(500\) \(-500\) \(0\)

This is the table of section 5.14.5 in all the numbers. The computation did not use statics, only the element matrices and assembly. The reaction of the clamp, \((\mat K\,\vek d - \vek f)\) in the rows of the node \(A\) (section 7.3.4), is the force \((0, -500, 0)\) N and the moment \((500, 0, -500)\) N m, which is opposite to the load: the moment of the force \(F\) about \(A\) is \(\vek r\times\vek F = (1, 0, 1)\times(0, 500, 0) = (-500, 0, 500)\) N m.

Figure 12.17 shows the frame and its deformed shape at \(50\) N, assembled from the Hermite fields of both elements. The column twists: the sections rotate about the axis \(Z\) by an angle that grows linearly from zero at the clamp to \(\varphi_{\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{B}} = 9{,}064\cdot 10^{-3}\) at \(B\).

Let us summarize. The space frame element is a bar element, a torsion element and two beam elements in separate groups of twelve unknowns (lemma 12.22). Turning the axes maps all the unknowns with the block \(\mat Q\), because the rotation vector behaves as a vector and not as a number (lemma 12.23). The rows of the assembled system are the joint equilibrium, the solution is unique and is a solution of the space frame exactly at the nodes, and for loads only at the nodes along the whole length (corollary 12.24). With the same procedure we computed what statics could not: the displacement of the point \(C\). In doing so we took the torsion constant \(J = 73\,178\) mm\(^4\) as data, and this data is the only thing that this section does not prove.

12.6 Constraints: multipliers and the penalty method

In section 12.4.5 we treated the roller support at \(C\) (definition 5.5) by prescribing one unknown, \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\). This works when the support closes the direction of a single coordinate, and chapter 7 showed how a prescribed unknown is eliminated (theorem 7.18). But what if the roller support at \(C\) does not stand on a horizontal base but on a base inclined at \(30°\) to the horizontal? By definition 5.5 the support moves freely along the base, but it cannot move in the direction of the normal \(\vek n = (-\sin 30°,\ \cos 30°)\) of the base. Only a combination of the displacements \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\) is forbidden, \(-\sin 30°\,u_{\mathrm{C}} + \cos 30°\,v_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\), and no coordinate is prescribed by itself. Chapter 7 announced that prescribed values can also be imposed by a penalty (kazenska metoda) and by Lagrange multipliers (Lagrangeevi množitelji), the penalty for frames in this chapter, while chapter 8 supplied the multipliers. This section carries both routes over to the finite element method and proves them in general form, for prescribed unknowns and for such combinations, because later in this chapter we shall meet a penalty that nobody added on purpose.

12.6.1 Linear constraints

We collect the unknowns of the system, the displacements and rotations of the nodes of the mesh, in a column \(\vek d\) with \(n\) entries. A condition like the ban on displacement in the direction of the normal is a linear equation for the entries of the column \(\vek d\). We write several such equations together.

Definition 12.25 Linear constraints and the constraint matrix (linearne vezi in matrika vezi)

Let \(\vek d\) be a column of \(n\) unknowns. Linear constraints (linearne vezi) are the equations

\[\mat C\,\vek d = \vek g , \tag{12.25}\]

where \(\mat C\) is a real matrix with \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns, \(m \le n\), that has \(m\) pivots (definition 8.20), and \(\vek g\) is a column of \(m\) given numbers. The matrix \(\mat C\) is called the constraint matrix (matrika vezi).

Source: COOK §13.1, equation (13.1-1) (PDF p. 503), where the constraint is written as \([C]\{D\} - \{Q\} = \{0\}\), and PDF p. 504: "[C] has more columns than rows", while the dependent unknowns are chosen so that their block is "square and nonsingular". The requirement of \(m\) pivots is our form of this condition, so that we can use lemma 8.35.

The condition on the pivots ensures two things, which we prove in theorem 12.26 (steps 1 and 3 of the proof): the constraints do not exclude each other, because the system (12.25) has a solution for every \(\vek g\), and no row is a combination of the others. The letter \(\mat C\) is the damping matrix in chapter 10, here it is the constraint matrix. Let us look at three examples on the L-frame of section 12.4.5, which after the clamp at \(A\) still has nine unknowns \(u_{\mathrm{B}}, v_{\mathrm{B}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{B}}, u_{\mathrm{D}}, v_{\mathrm{D}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{D}}, u_{\mathrm{C}}, v_{\mathrm{C}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{C}}\). The support in the direction \(\vek n\) is one constraint, \(m = 1\), with a row that has the numbers \(-\sin 30°\) and \(\cos 30°\) at the places of \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\), zero elsewhere, and \(g = 0\). A prescribed unknown \(d_{\mathrm{k}} = \bar d\) is a constraint with the row \(\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\) (the column \(\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\) has \(1\) at place \(k\) and zero elsewhere) and \(g = \bar d\). The clamp at \(A\) is three such rows with \(\bar d = 0\). A rigid link (toga palica) between the nodes \(B\) and \(C\) does not allow their distance to change. The points \(B\) and \(C\) lie on the same horizontal line, so for small displacements their distance changes by \(u_{\mathrm{C}} - u_{\mathrm{B}}\) and the rigid link is the constraint \(u_{\mathrm{B}} - u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\) with a row that has the numbers \(1\) and \(-1\) at the places of \(u_{\mathrm{B}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\). Figure 12.18 shows the frame with the support on the inclined base.

The condition on \(m\) pivots excludes rows that repeat the same requirement. Take the constraint \(d_1 + d_2 = 0\) and write it twice, the second time multiplied by \(2\): \(\mat C = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\), \(m = 2\). The second row is twice the first, so \(\mat C\) has one pivot and not two, and the condition of the definition does not hold. Let us see what breaks. For \(\vek g = (0, 0)\) the system has a solution, for example \(\vek d = \vek 0\), but \(\mat C^\T\vek\lambda = (\lambda_1 + 2\lambda_2)\,(1, 1)^\T\), so the equation \(\mat K\,\vek d^* = \vek f + \mat C^\T\vek\lambda\) determines only the sum \(\lambda_1 + 2\lambda_2\) and not \(\vek\lambda\) (step 3 of the proof of theorem 12.26 fails). For \(\vek g = (0, 1)\) the constraints demand \(d_1 + d_2 = 0\) and \(2(d_1 + d_2) = 1\), which exclude each other, and the set of constraints is empty (step 1 fails). This matrix differs from a support that is a single row in one thing: the same constraint is written twice.

How do we include such constraints in the system \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f\)? A route that stays within chapter 7 is local axes at the node: instead of \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\) we take as unknowns the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = \vek n\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) in the direction of the normal and the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{t}} = \vek t\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) along the base, \(\vek t = (\cos 30°, \sin 30°)\). The constraint is then the prescribed unknown \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\). This route works when the constraint concerns one node. For a rigid link between two nodes we have to express one unknown by the others, which is the general route that the proof of theorem 12.26 will use. Multipliers and the penalty instead add the constraints to the system without changing the unknowns, and they work for every constraint matrix.

12.6.2 Multipliers

The support in the direction \(\vek n\) acts on the frame with the force \(\lambda\,\vek n\) with an unknown number \(\lambda\), which the frame needs for equilibrium. Chapter 8 said this for every ideal constraint: the load of the constraint forces is a linear combination of the rows of the constraint matrix, \(\mat C^\T\vek\lambda\) (corollary 8.59). The unknowns are now \(\vek d\) and \(\vek\lambda\), and the equations are equilibrium \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f + \mat C^\T\vek\lambda\) and the constraints \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek g\). The sign is the sign of chapter 8: \(\mat C^\T\vek\lambda\) is the load that the constraints add to the external load \(\vek f\). We get the same system from energy: we seek the smallest value of the potential energy \(\Pi(\vek d) = \tfrac12\,\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d - \vek f^\T\vek d\) among the columns that satisfy the constraints. This is the linear case of theorem 8.36 with the gradient \(\mat K\,\vek d - \vek f\) of the function \(\Pi\) (symmetric \(\mat K\)) and with the rows of the matrix \(\mat C\) as the gradients of the constraints. The theorem tells when this route gives a single answer, and proves it without the implicit function theorem, because the constraints are linear.

Theorem 12.26 Minimum of the energy under linear constraints and multipliers (najmanjša energija pri linearnih vezeh in množitelji)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix of order \(n\) (definition 7.15), \(\vek f\) a column with \(n\) entries, \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek g\) linear constraints (definition 12.25), and \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d > 0\) for every column \(\vek d \ne \vek 0\) with \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek 0\). Then:

  1. The set of columns with \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek g\) is not empty, and the function \(\Pi(\vek d) = \tfrac12\,\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d - \vek f^\T\vek d\) has exactly one smallest value on it, at the column \(\vek d^*\).
  2. There is exactly one column \(\vek\lambda\) of \(m\) numbers with \(\mat K\,\vek d^* = \vek f + \mat C^\T\vek\lambda\). The column \(\mat C^\T\vek\lambda\) is the load of the constraint forces (corollary 8.59).
  3. The system
    \[\begin{pmatrix} \mat K & -\mat C^\T \\ -\mat C & \mat 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \vek d \\ \vek\lambda \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \vek f \\ -\vek g \end{pmatrix} \tag{12.26}\]
    is symmetric and has exactly one solution \((\vek d^*, \vek\lambda)\).
  4. If \(\mat K\) is positive definite, Gaussian elimination of the matrix of the system (12.26) without row exchanges has first \(n\) positive pivots, then \(m\) negative ones. After \(n\) steps the block \(\mat S = -\mat C\,\mat K^{-1}\mat C^\T\) remains. The matrix of the system is therefore not positive definite (lemma 8.62).
Proof

We have to show that the constraint set is not empty and that the energy on it is a strictly convex function of the free numbers, and then we obtain the multipliers from the lemma on linear multipliers. For part 4 we follow the elimination step by step.

  1. By definition 8.20 and the text after it we number the unknowns so that the pivot columns of the matrix \(\mat C\) come last, \(\vek d = (\vek y, \vek z)\), \(\mat C = [\mat C_{\mathrm{y}}\ \mat C_{\mathrm{z}}]\), and \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}\) is a square matrix of order \(m\) with \(m\) pivots, hence invertible (lemma 8.21). The numbering shuffles the entries of the columns \(\vek d\) and \(\vek f\) and the rows and columns of the matrix \(\mat K\) in the same way, so it changes neither the values of the function \(\Pi\) nor the assumptions nor the claims (as in step 1 of the proof of lemma 8.35). The equation \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek g\) is equivalent to \(\vek z = \mat C_{\mathrm{z}}^{-1}(\vek g - \mat C_{\mathrm{y}}\vek y)\). The constraint set is not empty: it contains \(\vek d_0 = (\vek 0, \mat C_{\mathrm{z}}^{-1}\vek g)\). For \(m = n\) there is no column \(\vek y\), \(\mat C = \mat C_{\mathrm{z}}\), and the constraint set is the single point \(\mat C^{-1}\vek g\). For \(m < n\) each of its points is \(\vek d_0 + \mat T\vek y\) with \(\mat T = \begin{pmatrix}\mat I \\ -\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}^{-1}\mat C_{\mathrm{y}}\end{pmatrix}\) and an arbitrary \(\vek y\). We have \(\mat C\,\mat T = \mat C_{\mathrm{y}} - \mat C_{\mathrm{z}}\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}^{-1}\mat C_{\mathrm{y}} = \mat 0\), and \(\mat T\vek y \ne \mat T\vek y'\) for \(\vek y \ne \vek y'\), because \(\mat T\) has the unit matrix on top.
  2. For \(m = n\) part 1 holds with \(\vek d^* = \mat C^{-1}\vek g\). Let \(m < n\). Multiplying out the products as in steps 1 to 3 of the proof of lemma 6.30, which use only the symmetry of the matrix \(\mat K\), gives \(\Pi(\vek d_0 + \mat T\vek y) = \tfrac12\,\vek y^\T\mat M\,\vek y - \vek h^\T\vek y + \Pi(\vek d_0)\) with \(\mat M = \mat T^\T\mat K\,\mat T\) and \(\vek h = \mat T^\T(\vek f - \mat K\vek d_0)\). The matrix \(\mat M\) is symmetric, and for \(\vek y \ne \vek 0\) we have \(\vek y^\T\mat M\,\vek y = (\mat T\vek y)^\T\mat K\,(\mat T\vek y) > 0\) by assumption, because \(\mat T\vek y \ne \vek 0\) and \(\mat C\,\mat T\vek y = \vek 0\). The matrix \(\mat M\) is therefore positive definite. By lemma 6.30 the function has exactly one smallest value, at the solution \(\vek y^*\) of the system \(\mat M\vek y = \vek h\) (the constant \(\Pi(\vek d_0)\) does not affect this), and since different \(\vek y\) give different points of the constraint set, \(\Pi\) has exactly one smallest value on the constraint set, at \(\vek d^* = \vek d_0 + \mat T\vek y^*\). This proves part 1.
  3. From \(\mat C^\T\vek x = \vek 0\) follows \(\vek x = \vek 0\). Indeed, the last \(m\) entries of the column \(\mat C^\T\vek x\) are \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}^\T\vek x\), and the matrix \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}^\T\) is invertible (lemma 8.21).
  4. Let \(\vek\delta\) be a column with \(\mat C\,\vek\delta = \vek 0\) and \(t\) any number. The column \(\vek d^* + t\vek\delta\) satisfies the constraints, so by the multiplied-out form of step 2 \(0 \le \Pi(\vek d^* + t\vek\delta) - \Pi(\vek d^*) = t\,a + \tfrac12\,t^2 b\) with \(a = (\mat K\vek d^* - \vek f)^\T\vek\delta\) and \(b = \vek\delta^\T\mat K\,\vek\delta \ge 0\). For \(a \ne 0\) and \(t = -a/(b + 1)\) the right side equals \(-a^2/(b + 1) + \tfrac12\,a^2 b/(b + 1)^2 = -a^2\,(b/2 + 1)/(b + 1)^2 < 0\), which is a contradiction. Hence \((\mat K\vek d^* - \vek f)\cdot\vek\delta = 0\) for every \(\vek\delta\) with \(\mat C\,\vek\delta = \vek 0\). For \(m < n\), by lemma 8.35 (with the column \(\mat K\vek d^* - \vek f\)) there is a \(\vek\lambda\) with \(\mat K\vek d^* - \vek f = \mat C^\T\vek\lambda\). For \(m = n\) such a \(\vek\lambda\) is \((\mat C^\T)^{-1}(\mat K\vek d^* - \vek f)\) (lemma 8.21). Two such \(\vek\lambda\) have a difference \(\vek x\) with \(\mat C^\T\vek x = \vek 0\), so by step 3 they are equal. This is part 2.
  5. The system (12.26) is symmetric, because \(\mat K\) is symmetric and \((-\mat C^\T)^\T = -\mat C\). Its rows are \(\mat K\vek d - \mat C^\T\vek\lambda = \vek f\) and \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek g\). The pair \((\vek d^*, \vek\lambda)\) satisfies them by step 4. Let \((\vek d, \vek\lambda')\) satisfy them too. For every \(\vek\delta\) with \(\mat C\,\vek\delta = \vek 0\), by the multiplied-out form of step 2,
    \[\begin{aligned} \Pi(\vek d + \vek\delta) - \Pi(\vek d) &= (\mat K\vek d - \vek f)^\T\vek\delta + \tfrac12\,\vek\delta^\T\mat K\,\vek\delta \\ &= \vek\lambda'^\T\mat C\,\vek\delta + \tfrac12\,\vek\delta^\T\mat K\,\vek\delta = \tfrac12\,\vek\delta^\T\mat K\,\vek\delta \ge 0 \end{aligned}\]
    and every point of the constraint set has the form \(\vek d + \vek\delta\). Hence \(\Pi\) has its smallest value on the constraint set at \(\vek d\), by step 2 \(\vek d = \vek d^*\), then \(\mat C^\T(\vek\lambda' - \vek\lambda) = \vek 0\) and by step 3 \(\vek\lambda' = \vek\lambda\). This is part 3.
  6. Let \(\mat K\) be positive definite. Steps 6 to 9 hold for the original numbering of the unknowns, since step 3 does not depend on the order of the entries of the column \(\mat C^\T\vek x\). From \(\mat K\vek w = \vek 0\) follows \(\vek w^\T\mat K\,\vek w = 0\) and \(\vek w = \vek 0\), so \(\mat K\) is invertible and \((\mat K^{-1})^\T = (\mat K^\T)^{-1} = \mat K^{-1}\) (lemma 8.21). For \(\vek y \ne \vek 0\) we have \(\vek w = \mat K^{-1}\vek y \ne \vek 0\) and \(\vek y^\T\mat K^{-1}\vek y = (\mat K\vek w)^\T\vek w = \vek w^\T\mat K\,\vek w > 0\). The matrix \(\mat K^{-1}\) is positive definite.
  7. Let \(\mat A\) be the matrix of the system (12.26). Step \(k\) of elimination without row exchanges subtracts from each row below row \(k\) the multiple of row \(k\) that makes a zero below pivot \(k\) (step 4 of the proof of theorem 6.29). In the first \(n\) steps the rows \(1, \dots, n\) change only by subtraction of multiples of rows \(1, \dots, n\), and the multipliers are ratios of entries of the upper left block of order \(n\). This block therefore changes exactly as in the elimination of the matrix \(\mat K\), and the pivots of the first \(n\) steps are the pivots of the matrix \(\mat K\), all positive by theorem 6.29.
  8. After the first \(n\) steps each row \(n + r\) is the original row \(n + r\) of the matrix \(\mat A\) minus a combination of the original rows \(1, \dots, n\), since by step 7 the changed rows \(1, \dots, n\) are also combinations of the original ones. The original rows \(1, \dots, n\) are \([\mat K\ \ {-\mat C^\T}]\), and the rows \(n + 1, \dots, n + m\) are \([-\mat C\ \ \mat 0]\). The lower rows are therefore \([-\mat C - \mat X\mat K\ \ \ \mat X\mat C^\T]\) for some matrix \(\mat X\) with \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns. The elimination has made zeros below the first \(n\) pivots, and later steps keep them, because they subtract rows that already have zeros in the earlier columns. Hence \(-\mat C - \mat X\mat K = \mat 0\), by multiplication with \(\mat K^{-1}\) from the right \(\mat X = -\mat C\,\mat K^{-1}\), and the remaining block is \(\mat X\mat C^\T = -\mat C\,\mat K^{-1}\mat C^\T = \mat S\).
  9. The matrix \(\mat S\) is symmetric by step 6 and lemma 1.101. For \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\) we have \(\vek x^\T(-\mat S)\,\vek x = (\mat C^\T\vek x)^\T\mat K^{-1}(\mat C^\T\vek x) > 0\) by steps 3 and 6, so \(-\mat S\) is positive definite and its elimination without row exchanges has \(m\) positive pivots (theorem 6.29). The elimination of the matrix \(\mat S\) has the same multipliers and in every step the opposite numbers, hence \(m\) negative pivots. The steps \(n + 1, \dots, n + m\) of the elimination of the matrix \(\mat A\) are the elimination of the block \(\mat S\), as in step 4 of the proof of theorem 6.29. Since some pivots are negative, the matrix \(\mat A\) is not positive definite by lemma 8.62. This is part 4.

Source: COOK §13.2 (PDF pp. 506-507, read): multipliers as constraint forces, equations (13.2-2), "The null submatrix in Eq. 13.2-2 becomes nonzero in the course of a Gauss elimination", "the solution process proceeds normally if [K] is by itself positive definite", the sign of the multiplier is not significant. The sign is ours, following chapter 8. The proof is not from a source.

The proof has shown that the constraints leave us a space \(\mat T\vek y\) of free numbers on which the energy is strictly convex, and that the multiplier is exactly the number that the lemma on linear multipliers requires. Steps 1 and 2 are also a computational procedure: we express the dependent unknowns by the free ones and solve the system \(\mat T^\T\mat K\,\mat T\,\vek y = \mat T^\T(\vek f - \mat K\vek d_0)\) of order \(n - m\) with a positive definite matrix. For prescribed unknowns \(\mat C_{\mathrm{y}} = \mat 0\), \(\mat T\) picks the free unknowns and the system is the reduced system of chapter 7 (COOK, PDF p. 504), while for constraints between several nodes we have to rearrange the matrix, which is laborious in programs (COOK, PDF p. 503). Part 4 tells what has happened to the matrix of the system (12.26): it is symmetric but no longer positive definite, so theorem 6.29 does not apply to it. With a positive definite matrix \(\mat K\) elimination without row exchanges still succeeds by part 4. With a singular matrix \(\mat K\) (a structure without supports, the supports being rows of the constraint matrix) it can fail: for our frame with all twelve unknowns, three rows of the clamp and the row of the normal, a zero pivot appears in the tenth step (NumPy), so rows have to be exchanged.

Let us test the theorem on the frame of section 12.4.5. First the roller support on a horizontal base at \(C\): the constraint \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\), the row \(\vek c^\T = \vek e_{\mathrm{v}_\mathrm{C}}^\T\), \(g = 0\). The matrix \(\mat K\) is the matrix of the nine free unknowns after the clamp at \(A\), positive definite. The system (12.26) gives \(\lambda = 226{,}59\) N. This is the reaction \(R = 226{,}590\) N of section 12.4.5: the reaction of a prescribed unknown was the value of \((\mat K\,\vek d - \vek f)\) in its row, which is \((\mat C^\T\vek\lambda)_{\mathrm{v}_\mathrm{C}} = \lambda\). By part 4 of the theorem the last pivot of the matrix of the system is the block \(\mat S = -\vek c^\T\mat K^{-1}\vek c\), computed as \(-6{,}378 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m/N, while the first nine pivots are positive, the smallest \(1{,}045 \cdot 10^4\). The number \(s = \vek c^\T\mat K^{-1}\vek c = 6{,}378 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m/N is the flexibility of the frame without the support at \(C\) in the direction \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\): \(\mat K^{-1}\vek c\) are the displacements due to a unit vertical force at \(C\), and \(\vek c^\T\) picks the vertical displacement of the point \(C\) from them. We computed the same frame with the clamp at \(A\) and the force \(500\) N at \(C\) in section 12.4.3, \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = -31{,}89\) mm, which is \(500\,s\). Without the support at \(C\) the force \(500\) N at \(D\) would lower the point \(C\) by \(14{,}45\) mm. The multiplier is the vertical force at \(C\) that lifts the point \(C\) back by exactly this amount: \(\lambda\,s = 14{,}45\) mm, \(\lambda = 14{,}45\ \text{mm}/s = 226{,}59\) N. The multiplier is thus the unknown that chapter 5 chose as the reaction \(R\) of the statically indeterminate frame, and the equation for \(\lambda\) is its condition that \(C\) does not move, except that the system now sets up the unknown and the condition by itself.

The hypothesis \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d > 0\) on the kernel of the matrix \(\mat C\) is not just a matter of style. Its negation is: there is \(\vek d \ne \vek 0\) with \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek 0\) and \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = 0\). Take \(n = 2\), \(\mat K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) (semidefinite, as the theorem allows), \(\mat C = (1\ \ 0)\), \(g = 1\) and \(\vek f = (0, 1)^\T\). The constraint determines \(d_1 = 1\), the kernel of \(\mat C\) consists of the columns \((0, t)^\T\), and for all of them \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = 0\), so the hypothesis does not hold. The energy on the set of constraints is \(\Pi(1, t) = 1 - t\), which decreases without bound, so there is no smallest value. The unknown \(d_2\) is held neither by a spring (\(K_{22} = 0\)) nor by a constraint, like a beam with a single hinge in corollary 12.11. For \(\mat K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0{,}01 \end{pmatrix}\) the hypothesis holds, because \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = 0{,}01\,t^2 > 0\) for \(t \ne 0\), and \(\Pi(1, t) = 1 + t^2/200 - t\) has its smallest value at \(t = 100\), \(\Pi = -49\).

The inclined base. The row \(\vek c^\T\) has the numbers \(-\sin 30° = -0{,}5\) and \(\cos 30° = 0{,}866\) at the places of \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\). The flexibility of the frame in the direction \(\vek n\) is \(s = \vek c^\T\mat K^{-1}\vek c = 7{,}254 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m/N, without the support \(C\) would move by \(15{,}51\) mm in the direction \(-\vek n\), and the multiplier is \(\lambda = 213{,}76\) N, again with \(\lambda\,s = 15{,}51\) mm. The support acts on the frame with the force \(\lambda\,\vek n = (-106{,}88,\ 185{,}13)\) N, which points up and to the left. The displacements are \(u_{\mathrm{C}} = -0{,}1533\) mm and \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = -0{,}0885\) mm. We check the constraint: \(-0{,}5\cdot(-0{,}1533) + 0{,}866\cdot(-0{,}0885) = 0{,}0767 - 0{,}0766 \approx 0\) within rounding. The displacement runs along the base, \(\vek t\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = -0{,}1770\) mm, down and to the left. With local axes at the node, the unknowns \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{t}}\) instead of \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\), the prescribed \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\) and the reduced system of chapter 7 we get the same displacements and the same force, \(213{,}76\) N in the row of the unknown \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) (NumPy). With all twelve unknowns and four rows (clamp, normal) we get from the singular matrix \(\mat K\) the same displacements and in addition the clamp forces \((106{,}88\ \text{N},\ 314{,}87\ \text{N},\ -42{,}01\ \text{N m})\) as the multipliers of the clamp rows. We check equilibrium: horizontally \(106{,}88 - 106{,}88 = 0\), vertically \(314{,}87 + 185{,}13 = 500\) N, the moment about \(A\) is \(-42{,}01 + 292{,}01 - 250{,}00 = 0\) N m (the support force gives \(1\cdot 185{,}13 + 1\cdot 106{,}88 = 292{,}01\) N m, the load \(-0{,}5\cdot 500\) N m).

Multipliers are exact and do not change the matrix \(\mat K\), but they have a price: the system has \(n + m\) unknowns and its matrix is not positive definite. A second way adds the constraints to the system in a way that keeps the size, the symmetry and positive definiteness.

12.6.3 The penalty method

Imagine that the support at \(C\) is not rigid, but that the node \(C\) is held by a very stiff spring of stiffness \(\alpha\) in the direction \(\vek n\), which is stretched by \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) when the node moves by \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) in the direction \(\vek n\). At \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\) the spring does not act, otherwise it stores the energy \(\tfrac12\,\alpha\,u_{\mathrm{n}}^2\). If the spring is stiff enough, \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) will be small. For a general constraint \(\mat C\,\vek d - \vek g\) is the column of the stretches of \(m\) springs, one for each row, and the energy of all springs is \(\tfrac12\,\alpha\,|\mat C\,\vek d - \vek g|^2\) (figure 12.19). COOK describes this on two bars: the spring has in effect added to the structure a bar of axial stiffness \(\alpha k\) ("has in effect added a bar of axial stiffness \(\alpha k\)", COOK, PDF p. 508), where \(k\) is the axial stiffness of a bar of the structure and \(\alpha\) a number without unit.

Definition 12.27 Penalty method and penalty number (kazenska metoda in kazensko število)

Let \(\mat K\), \(\vek f\) and the constraints \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek g\) be as in theorem 12.26 and let \(\alpha > 0\) be a real number, the penalty number (kazensko število). The penalty function is

\[\Pi_\alpha(\vek d) = \Pi(\vek d) + \tfrac12\,\alpha\,|\mat C\,\vek d - \vek g|^2 . \tag{12.27}\]

The penalty method (kazenska metoda) takes, instead of the solution \(\vek d^*\) of theorem 12.26, the penalty solution (kazenska rešitev) \(\vek d_\alpha\), the solution of the penalty system (kazenski sistem)

\[(\mat K + \alpha\,\mat C^\T\mat C)\,\vek d = \vek f + \alpha\,\mat C^\T\vek g . \tag{12.28}\]

The penalty forces (kazenske sile) are \(\vek\lambda_\alpha = -\alpha\,(\mat C\,\vek d_\alpha - \vek g)\), since (12.28) gives \(\mat K\,\vek d_\alpha = \vek f + \mat C^\T\vek\lambda_\alpha\), equilibrium with the spring forces in the form of theorem 12.26.

Source: COOK §13.3 (PDF pp. 507-508, read): (13.3-2) and (13.3-3) with a diagonal matrix of penalty numbers \([\alpha]\), we take a single number. The penalty forces are our notation.

We expand \(\tfrac12\,\alpha\,|\mat C\,\vek d - \vek g|^2 = \tfrac12\,\vek d^\T(\alpha\,\mat C^\T\mat C)\,\vek d - \alpha\,(\mat C^\T\vek g)^\T\vek d + \tfrac12\,\alpha\,|\vek g|^2\), so \(\Pi_\alpha\) is a quadratic function with the matrix \(\mat K + \alpha\,\mat C^\T\mat C\) and the right side \(\vek f + \alpha\,\mat C^\T\vek g\), and its smallest value solves (12.28) if this matrix is positive definite (lemma 6.30). The letter \(\alpha\) is the coefficient of thermal expansion in chapters 3 and 7, here it is the penalty number. For a prescribed unknown \(d_{\mathrm{k}} = \bar d\) with the row \(\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\) we have \(\alpha\,\mat C^\T\mat C = \alpha\,\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\): the penalty system adds \(\alpha\) to the diagonal entry \(K_{\mathrm{kk}}\) and \(\alpha\,\bar d\) to the right side of row \(k\), and changes no other number. This is the penalty by which, as chapter 7 announced (section 7.3.3), prescribed values can be imposed. How close is \(\vek d_\alpha\) to the true solution \(\vek d^*\), and how close are the penalty forces to the multipliers? The theorem gives the answer in general, and part 5 gives it for one constraint in closed form, which we then test on the frame.

Theorem 12.28 Error of the penalty method (napaka kazenske metode)

Let \(\mat K\), \(\vek f\), \(\mat C\), \(\vek g\) satisfy the hypotheses of theorem 12.26, and let \(\vek d^*\) and \(\vek\lambda\) be the solution and the multipliers of that theorem. Then the matrix \(\mat K + \mat C^\T\mat C\) is positive definite, its smallest eigenvalue \(\mu\) is positive, and:

  1. For every \(\alpha > 0\) the penalty system (12.28) has exactly one solution \(\vek d_\alpha\), which is the only minimum of the function \(\Pi_\alpha\).
  2. For every \(\alpha > 0\), \(|\mat C\,\vek d_\alpha - \vek g| \le |\vek\lambda|/\alpha\).
  3. For every \(\alpha > 0\), \((\vek d_\alpha - \vek d^*)^\T(\mat K + \alpha\,\mat C^\T\mat C)(\vek d_\alpha - \vek d^*) \le |\vek\lambda|^2/\alpha\), and for \(\alpha \ge 1\) also \(|\vek d_\alpha - \vek d^*| \le |\vek\lambda|/\sqrt{\mu\,\alpha}\).
  4. The penalty forces approach the multipliers: \(|\vek\lambda_\alpha - \vek\lambda| \le q\,|\vek\lambda|/\sqrt{\alpha}\) for \(\alpha \ge 1\), where \(q = n\,K_{\max}/\sqrt{\mu\,\nu}\), \(K_{\max}\) is the largest absolute value of the entries of the matrix \(\mat K\) and \(\nu\) is the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix \(\mat C\,\mat C^\T\), which is positive.
  5. If \(\mat K\) is positive definite, then for every \(\alpha > 0\) \(\vek d_\alpha - \vek d^* = -\mat K^{-1}\mat C^\T(\mat I + \alpha\,\mat C\,\mat K^{-1}\mat C^\T)^{-1}\vek\lambda\). For one constraint with the row \(\vek c^\T\), \(s = \vek c^\T\mat K^{-1}\vek c\) and \(\lambda \ne 0\)
    \[\begin{aligned} \vek d_\alpha - \vek d^* &= -\frac{\lambda}{1 + \alpha s}\,\mat K^{-1}\vek c , \\ &\qquad \lambda_\alpha = \lambda\,\frac{\alpha s}{1 + \alpha s} , \\ &\qquad \frac{\lambda_\alpha - \lambda}{\lambda} = -\frac{1}{1 + \alpha s} . \end{aligned} \tag{12.29}\]
Proof

We have to show first that the penalty system has exactly one solution, and then estimate the constraints, the energy and the forces from the equation for the error. The error \(\vek e = \vek d_\alpha - \vek d^*\) solves the system with the penalty matrix and the right side \(-\mat C^\T\vek\lambda\).

  1. The matrix \(\mat K + \mat C^\T\mat C\) is symmetric and \(\vek d^\T(\mat K + \mat C^\T\mat C)\vek d = \vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d + |\mat C\,\vek d|^2 \ge 0\). If the sum is zero, both nonnegative terms are zero, \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek 0\) and \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = 0\), so by hypothesis \(\vek d = \vek 0\). The matrix is positive definite, its smallest eigenvalue \(\mu\) is positive and \(\vek d^\T(\mat K + \mat C^\T\mat C)\vek d \ge \mu\,|\vek d|^2\) (theorem 10.26 with \(\mat M = \mat I\)). For \(\alpha \ge 1\), \(\vek d^\T(\mat K + \alpha\,\mat C^\T\mat C)\vek d = \vek d^\T(\mat K + \mat C^\T\mat C)\vek d + (\alpha - 1)\,|\mat C\,\vek d|^2 \ge \mu\,|\vek d|^2\), and for \(0 < \alpha < 1\) it is at least \(\alpha\,\vek d^\T(\mat K + \mat C^\T\mat C)\vek d\), because \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d \ge 0\). In both cases the penalty matrix is positive definite. By theorem 6.29 the system has exactly one solution, and by lemma 6.30 it is the smallest value of the function \(\Pi_\alpha\) (expansion below definition 12.27).
  2. We subtract \(\mat K\,\vek d^* = \vek f + \mat C^\T\vek\lambda\) from (12.28) and use \(\mat C\,\vek d^* = \vek g\): \(\mat K\,\vek e + \alpha\,\mat C^\T(\mat C\,\vek d_\alpha - \vek g) = -\mat C^\T\vek\lambda\), and \(\mat C\,\vek d_\alpha - \vek g = \mat C\,\vek e\). Hence
    \[(\mat K + \alpha\,\mat C^\T\mat C)\,\vek e = -\mat C^\T\vek\lambda . \tag{12.30}\]
  3. We multiply (12.30) by \(\vek e^\T\): \(\vek e^\T(\mat K + \alpha\,\mat C^\T\mat C)\vek e = -(\mat C\,\vek e)\cdot\vek\lambda \le |\mat C\,\vek e|\,|\vek\lambda|\) (Cauchy-Schwarz, lemma 8.23, part 1). Since \(\vek e^\T\mat K\,\vek e \ge 0\), the left side is at least \(\alpha\,|\mat C\,\vek e|^2\), hence \(\alpha\,|\mat C\,\vek e|^2 \le |\mat C\,\vek e|\,|\vek\lambda|\) and \(|\mat C\,\vek e| \le |\vek\lambda|/\alpha\). For \(\mat C\,\vek e = \vek 0\) this holds as well. Since \(\mat C\,\vek e = \mat C\,\vek d_\alpha - \vek g\), this is part 2.
  4. With the estimate of step 3, \(\vek e^\T(\mat K + \alpha\,\mat C^\T\mat C)\vek e \le |\mat C\,\vek e|\,|\vek\lambda| \le |\vek\lambda|^2/\alpha\), the first estimate of part 3. By step 1, for \(\alpha \ge 1\) the left side is at least \(\mu\,|\vek e|^2\), hence \(|\vek e|^2 \le |\vek\lambda|^2/(\mu\,\alpha)\). This is part 3.
  5. From (12.28) and (12.30), \(\mat C^\T(\vek\lambda_\alpha - \vek\lambda) = \mat K\,\vek d_\alpha - \mat K\,\vek d^* = \mat K\,\vek e\). By lemma 8.23, part 4, \(|\mat K\,\vek e| \le n\,K_{\max}\,|\vek e|\). The matrix \(\mat C\,\mat C^\T\) is symmetric and for \(\vek z \ne \vek 0\) we have \(\vek z^\T\mat C\,\mat C^\T\vek z = |\mat C^\T\vek z|^2 > 0\) by step 3 of the proof of theorem 12.26, so it is positive definite and its smallest eigenvalue \(\nu\) is positive. By theorem 10.26 with \(\mat M = \mat I\), \(|\mat C^\T\vek z|^2 \ge \nu\,|\vek z|^2\). For \(\vek z = \vek\lambda_\alpha - \vek\lambda\) and \(\alpha \ge 1\), by step 4 \(\sqrt{\nu}\,|\vek z| \le n\,K_{\max}\,|\vek e| \le n\,K_{\max}\,|\vek\lambda|/\sqrt{\mu\,\alpha}\), which is part 4.
  6. Let \(\mat K\) be positive definite and \(\mat W = \mat I + \alpha\,\mat C\,\mat K^{-1}\mat C^\T\). The matrix \(\mat W\) is symmetric and \(\vek z^\T\mat W\vek z = |\vek z|^2 + \alpha\,(\mat C^\T\vek z)^\T\mat K^{-1}(\mat C^\T\vek z) > 0\) for \(\vek z \ne \vek 0\) (\(\mat K^{-1}\) is symmetric and positive definite by step 6 of the proof of theorem 12.26). The matrix \(\mat W\) is positive definite, hence invertible (theorem 6.29 and lemma 8.21). We have \((\mat K + \alpha\,\mat C^\T\mat C)\,\mat K^{-1}\mat C^\T = \mat C^\T + \alpha\,\mat C^\T\mat C\,\mat K^{-1}\mat C^\T = \mat C^\T\mat W\). Therefore \(\vek e = -\mat K^{-1}\mat C^\T\mat W^{-1}\vek\lambda\) is a solution of equation (12.30), and the only one, because the penalty matrix is invertible. For \(m = 1\), \(\mat C = \vek c^\T\), \(\mat W = 1 + \alpha s\) is a number, and \(\lambda_\alpha - \lambda = -\alpha\,(\mat C\,\vek e) - \lambda = \alpha\,\lambda\,s/(1 + \alpha s) - \lambda = -\lambda/(1 + \alpha s)\), which gives (12.29).

Source: COOK §13.3 (PDF pp. 507-508, read): the example of two bars with the solution (13.3-6), in which the error is proportional to \(1/(1 + \alpha)\). The proof is not from a source, the estimates 2 to 4 do not appear in COOK.

The proof has shown three things. The violation of the constraints at the penalty number \(\alpha\) is at most \(|\vek\lambda|/\alpha\): the larger the force the constraint needs, the larger the stretch of the spring. The energy of the error measured with the penalty matrix, \(\tfrac12\,\vek e^\T(\mat K + \alpha\,\mat C^\T\mat C)\vek e\), falls like \(1/\alpha\). The estimate of the distance to the true solution falls only like \(1/\sqrt\alpha\), because we bound the energy from below with the smallest eigenvalue, that is for the worst direction. The estimate of part 4 tells only that the penalty forces converge to the multipliers, and its constant is crude: for our frame \(q = 9{,}7 \cdot 10^7\) (mixed units). For one constraint and a positive definite matrix \(\mat K\) the distance and the error of the force are truly proportional to \(1/\alpha\), as formula (12.29) tells, in which \(\alpha s\) is the ratio of the penalty stiffness \(\alpha\) to the stiffness \(1/s\) of the structure in the direction of the constraint: the error is small when the spring is much stiffer than the structure in that direction.

The horizontal base. For a given \(\alpha s\), by (12.29) \(\lambda_\alpha = \lambda\,\alpha s/(1 + \alpha s)\) and the violation is \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = -\lambda s/(1 + \alpha s)\). The computation (NumPy, penalty system with nine unknowns) confirms this formula to all digits:

The bound of part 2 of the theorem holds and is accurate to 1 % for \(\alpha s \ge 10^2\), because the violation is \(\lambda s/(1 + \alpha s)\) and the bound \(\lambda s/(\alpha s)\). At \(\alpha s = 1\) the spring is as stiff as the frame in the direction of the constraint and takes only half of the force that the constraint requires: \(\lambda_\alpha = 113{,}29 = \lambda/2\). At \(\alpha s = 10^2\) the left side of the first estimate of part 3 equals, by formula (12.29), \(\lambda^2 s/(1 + \alpha s) = 3{,}242 \cdot 10^{-2}\) N m, and the bound \(\lambda^2/\alpha\) is \(3{,}275 \cdot 10^{-2}\) N m. The bound of part 3 for the distance, \(|\vek d_\alpha - \vek d^*| \le |\vek\lambda|/\sqrt{\mu\alpha}\) with \(\mu = 3410\) (mixed units N/m, N and N m), is \(3{,}1 \cdot 10^{-3}\) at \(\alpha s = 10^2\), while the error is \(3{,}0 \cdot 10^{-4}\): the bound holds and is ten times too large.

The inclined base. The table shows the forces and the condition number (definition 6.31) of the matrix \(\mat K + \alpha\,\vek c\,\vek c^\T\) at chosen values of \(\alpha s\), \(s = 7{,}254 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m/N, with the exact value \(\lambda = 213{,}76458\) N. The condition number of the matrix \(\mat K\) without the support at \(C\) is \(2{,}76 \cdot 10^5\).
